preamble: LPCC COMPREHENSIVE SIMULATION - FORM B
143-Question Candidate Examination
Version 2.0 | August 2026 | Current-Format Edition | Exam Preparation Program | No CE Credit
CTA-APPROVED PRODUCTION MASTER - EXTERNAL SME/ETHICS RELEASE GATE PENDING

Form B is a fresh, original CTA simulation designed to approximate the reasoning demands, pacing, and progressive multi-section case format of the current NCMHCE. It is an educational review resource and is not an official NBCC, CCE, Pearson VUE, or California BBS examination.
CTA internal approval recorded August 15, 2026. External SME/ethics validation remains a separate release gate before learner publication.
Administration Instructions
Complete all 11 cases in one sitting when feasible.
Use 225 minutes for the examination questions, with one 15-minute scheduled break after Case 5.
Each case is divided into three sections. In simulation mode, review within the current section only. After advancing, do not return to prior sections or completed cases.
Select one best answer for every question and do not leave items blank.
Record confidence from 1 (guessing) to 5 (high confidence) for later remediation.
Do not open the controlled answer-and-rationales form until the examination is complete.
This is the current-format edition. CTA must review and update the simulation before use with examinations administered under the revised NCMHCE specifications effective July 1, 2027.

Form B contains 11 three-part cases and 143 questions. The controlled scoring map contains 100 scored-style items distributed to the current NCMHCE domains and 43 field-test-style items. Field-test-style items are not identified in the candidate form; answer every item.

Record the testing conditions and your subjective experience before opening the controlled rationales. This helps distinguish content gaps from pacing, fatigue, confidence, or question-reading errors.
Candidates remain responsible for reviewing the current NBCC NCMHCE candidate materials and any applicable California BBS LPCC examination requirements before scheduling or testing.

sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which inquiry would most directly determine whether Lena needs immediate protective intervention?

options.a: Clarify the images’ frequency, triggers, meaning, and any checking, avoidance, or reassurance that follows.
options.b: Review postpartum pain, bleeding, thyroid symptoms, medications, and reasons for the missed medical visit.
options.c: Assess suicidal thinking, infant-harm intent, psychotic or manic symptoms, and Lena’s present caregiving capacity.
options.d: Map nighttime caregiving, available support, total sleep, and the partner’s observations of daily functioning.

questions.question_text: Which provisional formulation is best supported by the information available in this section?

options.a: Provisional psychotic disorder, pending observation of whether insight fluctuates and whether unusual beliefs or perceptual disturbances emerge.
options.b: Provisional obsessive-compulsive disorder, pending clarification of whether mood and sleep symptoms are secondary to obsessions or reflect a co-occurring depressive episode.
options.c: Provisional major depressive disorder with peripartum onset; obsessive-compulsive, bipolar, psychotic, and medical explanations for the presentation remain under assessment.
options.d: Provisional adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood, pending clarification of symptom severity, duration, and functional impairment.

questions.question_text: While arranging postpartum medical follow-up, which additional psychiatric history would most change both the working diagnosis and the initial treatment pathway?

options.a: Prior trauma followed by reexperiencing, hyperarousal, dissociation, or avoidance during pregnancy or childbirth.
options.b: Previous elevated or irritable mood, reduced need for sleep, impulsive behavior, or grandiosity.
options.c: Previous depressive episodes linked to major losses, role transitions, relationship stress, or seasonal patterns.
options.d: Intrusive thoughts before pregnancy that led to checking, mental rituals, avoidance, or repeated reassurance.

questions.question_text: Lena says, “What kind of mother thinks something like this?” Which response best combines empathic attunement with continued assessment?

options.a: Sleep loss can intensify unwanted thoughts, so let’s stabilize your sleep before examining what the image means.
options.b: The image sounds frightening and shame-filled. What happens when it appears, and what do you fear it means?
options.c: Your distress suggests the image is not an intention, so we can focus now on the depressive symptoms.
options.d: Protecting your baby matters deeply to you. I can explain why unwanted thoughts are common after childbirth.

sections.stem:
Lena is 32 and six weeks postpartum. For the past month, she has felt sad or tearful most days, lost interest in activities, felt intense guilt, had low energy and difficulty concentrating, and remained awake even when the baby sleeps.

She reports sudden, vivid images of accidentally dropping the baby while walking near the staircase. She experiences the images as unwanted and frightening, avoids carrying the baby near the stairs, and asks her partner to do so. Lena denies wanting to harm the baby and says, “What kind of mother thinks something like this?”

Her partner reports increasing withdrawal. Lena is breastfeeding and has not attended a postpartum medical visit.

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: After immediate safety and medical steps are arranged, which intervention plan best fits the clarified presentation?

options.a: Use CBT with graded exposure and response prevention, while treating depression and coordinating perinatal medical care.
options.b: Use cognitive restructuring of catastrophic interpretations and ask the partner to provide limited reassurance during early practice.
options.c: Use supportive therapy and partner sessions, reserving structured behavioral work for symptoms that persist after stabilization.
options.d: Begin behavioral activation and protected-sleep planning, postponing direct work with the intrusive images until mood symptoms remit.

questions.question_text: Which safety-plan structure is most proportionate to Lena’s current presentation?

options.a: Emphasize partner observation, temporary transfer of infant care, and same-day reassessment whenever any intrusive image becomes more intense.
options.b: Prioritize protected sleep, partner support, and increased session frequency, reserving emergency criteria for changes in intent or behavior.
options.c: Focus on reasons for living, weekly monitoring, and Lena’s agreement to contact the counselor before taking unsafe action.
options.d: Name warning signs, coping steps, supportive contacts, crisis resources, and specific thresholds for urgent evaluation or emergency care.

questions.question_text: Lena says her family values private self-reliance in motherhood and places strong meaning on breastfeeding. Which inquiry BEST clarifies how these expectations should influence treatment?

options.a: Ask whether Lena wants her partner to explain the family's expectations so the counselor can understand caregiving beliefs before setting goals.
options.b: Ask Lena which family, cultural, spiritual, or feeding expectations feel supportive, burdensome, or not personally meaningful and how she wants them addressed.
options.c: Explore how postpartum norms in Lena's community may influence shame and help-seeking, then offer possible themes for Lena to endorse or reject.
options.d: Focus first on how family expectations affect adherence and functioning, deferring broader identity meanings until Lena's symptoms and sleep are more stable.

questions.question_text: Lena wants both her partner and prescriber involved. Which information-sharing plan is most appropriate?

options.a: Use one broad authorization so the partner and prescriber receive the same summary and future treatment updates.
options.b: Have Lena relay clinical updates herself while the counselor documents recommendations without contacting either party.
options.c: Authorize communication with the prescriber and let Lena decide informally what her partner should know between sessions.
options.d: Clarify each recipient’s role, obtain purpose-specific authorization, and limit disclosure to information needed for the agreed coordination.

questions.question_text: What is the best working hypothesis about repeated reassurance between Lena and her partner?

options.a: It briefly reduces distress while reinforcing the idea that certainty is required before Lena can resume infant care.
options.b: It provides emotional co-regulation that should continue until Lena completes her first in-vivo exposure successfully.
options.c: It is neutral support; avoidance should be targeted before the counselor modifies the partner’s responses.
options.d: It can be reduced after mood improves, because changing it now could weaken partner involvement and increase shame.

sections.stem:
Direct assessment reveals passive thoughts that her family might be better off without her, but no plan, intent, preparatory behavior, or past suicide attempt. Lena denies any wish or intent to harm the baby.

She recognizes the images as products of her own mind, resists them, and reports no voices, commands, fixed beliefs, disorganization, elevated or irritable mood, grandiosity, or reduced need for sleep. She feels exhausted and wants sleep.

When distressed, Lena repeatedly asks her partner to promise that she is not dangerous. The reassurance helps briefly, but the doubt returns. Lena’s sister was hospitalized for postpartum psychosis.

Lena says her family values private self-reliance in motherhood and views breastfeeding as a sign of being a good mother. She is unsure how much those expectations reflect her own values.

Her partner can help with nighttime care and agrees to participate in a safety and support plan. Lena is willing to authorize coordination with her obstetric clinician and a psychiatric prescriber.

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: Lena and the counselor are establishing the next phase of treatment. Which objective is BEST matched to her current progress and remaining impairment?

options.a: Maintain mild depressive symptoms for four weeks and contact the prescriber if mood, sleep, or intrusive-thought distress increases.
options.b: Over four weeks, progress through agreed safe infant-care steps near the stairs while reducing reassurance and continuing mood, sleep, and safety monitoring.
options.c: Resume full independent stair carrying within two weeks while maintaining the sleep plan and using partner support only when distress becomes severe.
options.d: Reduce intrusive-image frequency by seventy-five percent before decreasing partner assistance with infant care or moving toward more difficult behavioral tasks.

questions.question_text: Which behavioral strategy is the best next step for the remaining avoidance?

options.a: Build a hierarchy of objectively safe infant-care steps, reduce reassurance rituals, and repeat each step for new learning.
options.b: Use imaginal rehearsal at first, because in-vivo practice near stairs creates avoidable risk to the infant.
options.c: Practice the full staircase task with the partner nearby, using sustained distress reduction as the criterion for success.
options.d: Maintain partner-led stair use while strengthening relaxation, then begin exposure after several weeks without intrusive images.

questions.question_text: Which data set would provide the strongest evidence that counseling is producing meaningful change?

options.a: Repeated depression scores, session attendance, medication follow-through, and Lena’s satisfaction with counseling.
options.b: Repeated intrusive-thought ratings, partner observations of stair use, and the counselor’s estimate of Lena’s insight.
options.c: Repeated mood and anxiety scores, risk status, sleep, reassurance seeking, and behaviorally defined infant-care functioning.
options.d: Repeated sleep and functioning ratings, obstetric follow-up, and whether Lena reports fewer distressing images.

questions.question_text: Which termination discussion is MOST appropriate before scheduled counseling ends?

options.a: Set a fixed schedule of monthly booster sessions before termination so symptom recurrence can be detected early and managed within the existing relationship.
options.b: Ask Lena's partner to assume primary monitoring for recurrence after counseling ends and contact the counselor if Lena's functioning changes.
options.c: Keep the case open until Lena decides whether she wants another pregnancy because future perinatal stress could reactivate symptoms.
options.d: Review gains, feelings about ending, warning signs, supports, remaining provider follow-up, and how Lena can re-enter care if clinically indicated.

sections.stem:
Eight weeks later, Lena has completed medical and psychiatric evaluations. No psychotic or manic symptoms have emerged. She continues coordinated treatment.

Her depressive symptoms have decreased from severe to mild, she has had no passive suicidal thoughts for five weeks, and she usually sleeps six hours with the support plan. The intrusive images are less frequent and less distressing.

Lena now completes most infant-care tasks independently and can stand near the staircase while holding the baby, but her partner still carries the baby on the stairs. Lena occasionally seeks reassurance before infant-care tasks and says, “I want my independence back, but I’m afraid one bad image means I’m not ready.”

sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which follow-up would most directly clarify the mechanism maintaining Omar’s symptoms?

options.a: Review medical conditions, medications, dermatologic history, sleep, appetite, caffeine use, and other physical contributors affecting Omar now.
options.b: Trace one episode from trigger through feared consequence, ritual, relief, renewed doubt, time cost, and functional impact.
options.c: Explore graduate-school stress, family expectations, academic workload, social withdrawal, and supports available since symptoms began.
options.d: Assess depressive symptoms, hopelessness, suicide risk, prior treatment, family psychiatric history, and recent changes in functioning.

questions.question_text: Which provisional diagnosis is best supported by the information available in this section?

options.a: Generalized anxiety disorder, because illness and moral concerns occur across settings and interfere with school and worship.
options.b: Illness anxiety disorder, because contamination fears persist despite Omar recognizing that the objective danger may be limited.
options.c: Delusional disorder, because Omar continues to fear illness and moral harm despite feedback that the rituals are excessive.
options.d: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, with contamination and moral or religious obsessions followed by washing, prayer, and reassurance compulsions.

questions.question_text: Which inquiry would most directly clarify the relationship between Omar’s faith and the current symptoms?

options.a: Ask whether Omar wants a faith leader involved and what questions he would want that consultation to address.
options.b: Ask which family and community expectations shape Omar’s views of purity, morality, illness, help-seeking, and professional treatment.
options.c: Ask how Omar distinguishes chosen faith practices from repetitions driven by fear, doubt, or a need for certainty.
options.d: Ask how Omar’s spiritual beliefs have supported coping, identity, belonging, and decision-making during other stressful periods.

questions.question_text: Omar asks, “Are you going to tell me my faith is irrational?” Which response BEST demonstrates a nonjudgmental stance?

options.a: I will not evaluate your beliefs; we can focus on washing and leave religion outside treatment unless you later ask to discuss it.
options.b: I want to understand your beliefs, and we can compare your practices with common teachings in your faith before deciding what is symptom-driven.
options.c: I respect your faith. Would it help to involve a faith leader early so we do not misinterpret the religious material in treatment?
options.d: I want to understand what your faith means to you and when repetition is driven by fear or certainty, without deciding your beliefs.

sections.stem:
Omar is a 27-year-old graduate student. During the past 18 months, he has developed increasing fears of contamination and moral wrongdoing.

Touching shared door handles or religious objects can trigger thoughts that he may contract an illness, spread contamination to another person, or offend God. He responds by washing, showering, or repeating prayers until they feel “exactly right.” The rituals provide temporary relief, but doubt returns and he often begins the sequence again.

Omar now spends three to four hours each day completing these behaviors. He has missed classes, submitted work late, stopped attending communal worship, and developed cracked and irritated skin from washing.

Before these symptoms began, Omar describes prayer as flexible, time-limited, and personally meaningful. He now experiences much of the repetition as driven by fear and a need for certainty. He recognizes that the rituals appear excessive but says, “What if the one time I resist is the time something terrible happens?”

Omar reports no hallucinations, fixed unusual beliefs, manic symptoms, substance use, or current thoughts of harming himself or another person.

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Which initial intervention design best fits Omar’s presentation and stated values?

options.a: Build a collaborative hierarchy of objectively safe, values-consistent triggers and practice exposure while preventing washing, repeated prayer, and reassurance.
options.b: Begin by disputing feared moral consequences, adding exposure after Omar agrees that the feared outcomes are objectively unlikely.
options.c: Ask the faith leader to approve each exposure, then practice those tasks while Omar resists washing and repeated prayer.
options.d: Begin with Omar’s highest-rated contamination and worship tasks so he learns rapidly that intense distress can be tolerated.

questions.question_text: How should the counselor use Omar’s severe symptom-measure result in treatment planning?

options.a: Treat the score as confirmation that ERP is required and use it to set a standard weekly exposure dose.
options.b: Repeat the measure before discussing treatment because one severe score cannot appropriately inform any initial clinical decision.
options.c: Explain that the score reflects current severity, combine it with interview and functioning data, and identify Omar’s priorities.
options.d: Use the score primarily to determine whether Omar needs a higher level of care before outpatient treatment begins.

questions.question_text: Which faith-leader consultation plan best supports culturally responsive treatment?

options.a: With Omar’s consent, clarify which practices are customary or flexible while retaining clinical responsibility and avoiding exposure-by-exposure reassurance.
options.b: With Omar’s consent, ask the faith leader to review the hierarchy and approve each step as morally acceptable before practice.
options.c: With Omar’s consent, ask the faith leader to address guilt spiritually while limiting ERP to contamination-related washing behaviors.
options.d: With Omar’s consent, ask whether the repetitions are customary and use that judgment as the primary diagnostic evidence.

questions.question_text: Given the counselor’s current background, which professional response is most appropriate?

options.a: Seek qualified ERP supervision, discuss the limitation with Omar, and use co-treatment or referral until competence is established.
options.b: Proceed with ERP using the workshop materials, while reviewing outcomes and seeking specialist consultation only if progress stalls.
options.c: Provide supportive CBT for now, while Omar independently decides whether to pursue specialty ERP with another provider.
options.d: Refer Omar immediately and avoid any treatment role, because introductory training cannot contribute to future specialty competence.

sections.stem:
Further assessment reveals no evidence of psychosis or mania. Omar reports periods of discouragement but no current suicidal thinking, plan, intent, or history of suicidal behavior.

A validated obsessive-compulsive symptom measure indicates severe impairment. Omar’s primary goals are to resume communal worship, reduce the time spent completing rituals, protect his hands from further injury, and finish the academic term.

Omar’s family frequently answers questions such as, “Do you think I contaminated something?” and, “Was that prayer sincere enough?” Family members also complete some household tasks for him to prevent distress. The reassurance and assistance reduce anxiety briefly, but Omar soon seeks additional certainty.

Omar wants his faith respected during treatment and is open to exposure and response prevention. He is concerned, however, that a poorly designed exposure might require him to violate a genuine religious value. He authorizes a limited consultation with a faith leader to clarify customary and flexible practices. He does not want the faith leader to diagnose him or decide whether every exposure is morally safe.

The counselor has general CBT experience and has completed one introductory ERP workshop but has not treated an OCD case under supervision. A clinician with advanced OCD experience is available for structured consultation, supervision, co-treatment, or referral.

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: Omar asks, “Was that exposure morally safe?” Which response best demonstrates empathic attunement without reinforcing reassurance seeking?

options.a: Yes, the plan was values-consistent; remind yourself of that conclusion whenever moral doubt returns during practice.
options.b: You worked hard and felt frightened. Let’s examine what you learned without making me the source of certainty.
options.c: That sounds like the OCD seeking certainty; avoid discussing the moral concern further and return to the hierarchy.
options.d: Your anxiety rose sharply, so we should suspend worship exposures until you feel more certain about continuing.

questions.question_text: Which data set would provide the strongest evidence of meaningful treatment change?

options.a: Repeat the OCD measure and track ritual time, reassurance, avoidance, exposure completion, skin health, and school or worship functioning.
options.b: Track peak and ending distress for each exposure, ritual delay, and Omar’s confidence that every task was completed correctly.
options.c: Repeat the OCD measure and track ritual time, but omit worship functioning so religious practice is not pathologized.
options.d: Track school attendance, skin healing, and treatment satisfaction, using symptom measures only when Omar reports clear worsening.

questions.question_text: During a collaborative progress review, which summary BEST reflects Omar's treatment data?

options.a: ERP is not working well enough because the spike in anxiety and skipped practice show that the hierarchy has moved beyond Omar's readiness.
options.b: The principal goals are nearly met because ritual time and school functioning improved; reassurance can be addressed after the current hierarchy is completed.
options.c: There is meaningful progress in ritual time and functioning, while reassurance and inconsistent worship practice remain active barriers to review with Omar.
options.d: Outcome cannot be interpreted yet because the full hierarchy has not been completed; continue the current plan before drawing conclusions about progress.

questions.question_text: Which response would best facilitate Omar’s motivation to continue change?

options.a: Elicit Omar’s reasons for reclaiming worship and school, explore his exposure concerns, and choose one feasible next step.
options.b: Review the progress data and explain that stopping now would probably reverse gains and strengthen the obsessive-compulsive cycle.
options.c: Emphasize that ERP is first-line treatment and ask Omar to commit to six more sessions before reconsidering the approach.
options.d: Offer a temporary reassurance agreement so Omar can complete exposures until confidence and motivation improve.

questions.question_text: Which follow-up is MOST clinically useful?

options.a: Repeat a full diagnostic intake before discussing functioning so any recurrence can be distinguished from a new anxiety, mood, or spiritual concern.
options.b: Review ritual and reassurance drift, school and worship functioning, independent ERP use, current stressors, and whether booster or renewed care is needed.
options.c: Determine whether Omar has remained symptom-free since discharge before discussing current stressors, because residual symptoms would indicate incomplete termination.
options.d: Obtain collateral reports from family and the faith leader before reviewing Omar's own experience so maintenance can be verified across settings.

sections.stem:
Omar selects co-treatment with the OCD specialist while the counselor receives qualified ERP supervision.

Eight weeks later, Omar’s obsessive-compulsive symptom score has decreased from the severe to the moderate range. His daily ritual time has fallen from approximately three and a half hours to 75–90 minutes. He is attending classes consistently, his hands are healing, and he has attended part of a communal worship service.

Omar has completed several lower- and middle-level hierarchy tasks. Reassurance seeking remains frequent, however, and his family sometimes completes tasks or provides repeated answers when he becomes distressed.

During one worship-related exposure, Omar’s anxiety rose more than expected. He asked both the counselor and his mother to confirm that the exposure was morally safe and then skipped the next planned practice. He says, “Maybe this means ERP is wrong for me.”

No new suicide-risk, psychotic, manic, substance-related, or acute medical concerns have emerged.

sections.title: SECTION 1 - INITIAL PRESENTATION
sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which assessment approach would provide the strongest foundation for the initial formulation?

options.a: Interview Caleb about nausea and school fears, then use his account as the primary basis for the initial formulation.
options.b: Review teacher reports and school records first, then use caregiver interviews mainly to confirm the school-based pattern.
options.c: Build a developmental timeline using Caleb, both caregivers, school staff, pediatric records, sleep, symptoms, settings, and functioning.
options.d: Administer broad behavior scales to each informant, then focus the clinical interview on whichever domain receives the highest scores.

questions.question_text: Which explanation of counseling roles is most appropriate under the facts provided?

options.a: Define Caleb and both caregivers as joint clients, making treatment decisions and session information equally accessible to all three.
options.b: Define Caleb as the client, seek his assent, clarify caregiver roles and updates, and set boundaries for school communication.
options.c: Define the caregivers as collateral supports, sharing goals and progress while reserving all session content for Caleb.
options.d: Let the caregivers negotiate information access first, then document their agreement as the confidentiality plan governing treatment.

questions.question_text: Which approach BEST supports a culturally responsive understanding of the family's disagreement about Caleb's difficulties?

options.a: Explore Caleb's perspective first and ask the caregivers to explain their differences after the initial formulation so early assessment remains less conflictual.
options.b: Ask each caregiver how family values, school experiences, discipline, disability, and help-seeking shape their view, then identify shared goals before discussing disagreements.
options.c: Invite Caleb and each caregiver to describe how family experience, school expectations, discipline, disability, and help-seeking shape their perspectives without requiring agreement.
options.d: Explore structural school factors and prior experiences with institutions before asking about family meanings because systems may be shaping the disagreement most strongly.

questions.question_text: Which assessment strategy would best support the differential diagnosis?

options.a: Use one broad child-behavior scale with both caregivers, interpreting score differences as evidence about which account is more accurate.
options.b: Use child anxiety and somatic scales, allowing Caleb’s report to control the formulation when caregiver accounts remain inconsistent.
options.c: Use caregiver and teacher attention scales, treating cross-setting agreement as sufficient evidence that ADHD explains the school problems.
options.d: Combine child and caregiver anxiety reports, caregiver and teacher attention ratings, school records, and interviews interpreted with functional data.

sections.stem:
Caleb is a 10-year-old fifth-grade student. During the past seven weeks, he has increasingly complained of stomachaches on school mornings, cried or delayed when it is time to leave home, missed two to three school days each week, left assignments incomplete, and requested frequent visits to the school nurse.

A pediatric evaluation found no acute medical explanation. The pediatric clinician recommended routine follow-up and reassessment if Caleb develops new symptoms or other medical warning signs.

Caleb says he is afraid he will feel nauseated, vomit in class, and be laughed at by other students. His mother reports that Caleb has been distractible, disorganized, and prone to losing materials since early elementary school. His father notes that Caleb can concentrate for long periods on preferred activities and believes inconsistent discipline contributes to the problem.

Caleb’s parents are separated. Both have authority to participate in treatment decisions and receive the general progress information described in the counseling agreement. Their communication is conflictual, and they sometimes use Caleb to relay messages. They disagree about whether the primary problem is anxiety or insufficient discipline.

Caleb asks the counselor, “Are you going to tell them everything I say? Are you going to send it to my school?”

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Which provisional formulation best accounts for the available evidence?

options.a: Specific phobia, other type, focused on vomiting and driving school avoidance, with provisional ADHD requiring continued assessment.
options.b: Social anxiety disorder centered on public embarrassment, with a separate attention disorder still requiring longitudinal assessment.
options.c: Separation anxiety disorder with school refusal, while inattention is likely amplified by sleep loss and conflict between caregivers.
options.d: Somatic symptom disorder centered on nausea, with attention problems likely resulting from repeated symptom monitoring and missed instruction.

questions.question_text: Which initial intervention is best aligned with Caleb’s developmental level and current formulation?

options.a: Use verbal cognitive restructuring with drawings, asking Caleb to challenge nausea predictions before beginning any school-based practice.
options.b: Create a visual fear ladder, rehearse brief coping skills, and coordinate graded attendance with caregivers and school staff.
options.c: Stabilize sleep and classroom attention supports first, postponing graded school practice until nausea and anticipatory fear decrease.
options.d: Begin full-day attendance with a reward plan, adding coping rehearsal only if distress remains high after several school days.

questions.question_text: Caleb points to the volcano in his drawing and says, “This is what happens when everybody starts arguing.” Which response best uses listening and reflection?

options.a: Your parents’ disagreement is adding pressure; let’s decide which explanation best matches what happens before school.
options.b: The nausea feels real, and you fear classmates’ reactions and your parents’ conflict. Show me where it begins.
options.c: The medical visit found no illness, so let’s use your drawing to identify evidence that school is safe.
options.d: You want help with the nausea, but nurse visits may keep the fear going. Let’s plan a different response.

questions.question_text: Which explanation best describes the current family-school interactional pattern?

options.a: Nurse visits provide graded contact with school, so they should remain freely available while Caleb’s attendance improves.
options.b: Caregiver conflict heightens Caleb’s distress, so improving coparenting should precede direct work with school avoidance and nausea.
options.c: Nausea prompts checking, reassurance, nurse visits, or pickup; immediate relief may strengthen future escape while the symptoms remain genuine.
options.d: Morning reassurance lowers arousal, so caregivers should continue it consistently until Caleb can use coping skills independently at school.

sections.stem:
Separate interviews, school records, and rating scales provide additional information.

Caleb reports that he has feared vomiting for more than a year, but the fear did not substantially interfere with school until a classmate vomited in class two months ago. Since then, Caleb has become increasingly afraid that he will feel nauseated, vomit in front of classmates, and be laughed at.

Caleb does not report a broad fear of talking with peers, answering questions, eating in public, or being observed in other situations. He does not fear separating from either caregiver once he is at activities he enjoys. Screening reveals no reported bullying, trauma exposure, depressive syndrome, abuse, self-harm thoughts, or psychotic symptoms.

School records document forgetfulness, lost materials, incomplete work, delayed task initiation, and repeated need for redirection beginning in second grade—before the recent escalation in school avoidance. Similar organizational problems occur at both caregivers’ homes. Caregiver and teacher attention-rating scales show elevated inattentive symptoms. Child and caregiver anxiety measures show elevated fear related to vomiting and school attendance.

Caleb usually sleeps approximately seven hours, uses a tablet in bed, and stays up substantially later on weekends. His reading fluency is below the expected classroom range, but no formal learning evaluation has been completed.

Caleb participates more fully when allowed to draw. He draws his stomach as a volcano and says the worst parts are “throwing up where everybody can see” and “Mom and Dad fighting about me.”

When Caleb feels nauseated, he checks his body repeatedly and asks whether he is about to vomit. At school, he requests the nurse. At home, one caregiver repeatedly reassures him and sometimes allows him to remain home after continued complaints. The other caregiver insists that he attend and adds consequences when he resists. Nurse visits, pickup, or permission to remain home reduce Caleb’s distress immediately, but his fear is often stronger the following morning.

Both caregivers agree to participate in counseling and school coordination.

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: Which factor currently presents the clearest barrier to Caleb’s attendance goal?

options.a: Inconsistent caregiver responses, because absences cluster on mornings when reassurance ends with permission to remain home.
options.b: Academic backlog, because unfinished assignments make remaining at school more difficult than completing work at home.
options.c: Residual sleep inconsistency, because his weekend bedtime remains later than the routine used on school nights.
options.d: Residual fear of vomiting, because Caleb still reports nausea on most mornings despite lower anxiety scores.

questions.question_text: Which conclusion BEST describes Caleb's current level of mental health functioning?

options.a: Caleb's functioning is now broadly age-appropriate because attendance and sleep improved; remaining academic problems are most likely consequences of missed instruction.
options.b: Anxiety remains the primary functional impairment because Caleb still reports nausea and occasionally remains home despite improved attendance and nurse use.
options.c: Anxiety-related school functioning has improved substantially, while cross-setting attention, organization, and academic impairment remain clinically significant and require further assessment.
options.d: Current functioning cannot be interpreted reliably until the ADHD and learning evaluations are completed because anxiety and academic problems still overlap.

questions.question_text: How should the counselor respond to the school’s request for Caleb’s full counseling record?

options.a: Provide diagnosis, scores, and progress notes, but withhold Caleb’s drawings and statements about caregiver conflict.
options.b: Release the full record under the signed authorization, allowing school staff to determine which clinical details affect accommodations.
options.c: Decline direct communication to protect Caleb’s privacy, while asking the caregivers to convey the treatment recommendations.
options.d: Review the school’s purpose and authorization, involve Caleb, then send a focused summary of functioning and needed supports.

questions.question_text: Which conflict-resolution plan best supports consistent implementation across households?

options.a: Set a shared attendance goal, agree on one nausea response and medical thresholds, and use an adult-only communication plan.
options.b: Ask each caregiver to defend the preferred explanation, then negotiate a shared account before revising the agreed morning plan.
options.c: Assign one caregiver medical decisions and the other attendance decisions, with Caleb carrying updates between households.
options.d: Develop separate morning plans for each household, then compare which approach produces better attendance over two weeks.

questions.question_text: How should the counselor interpret Caleb’s persistent attention and academic difficulties?

options.a: ADHD is confirmed because attention ratings remain elevated after anxiety, sleep, and attendance have improved.
options.b: Further ADHD and learning assessment is warranted because cross-setting impairment predates anxiety and persists after initial improvement.
options.c: Attention symptoms were secondary to anxiety because Caleb’s school attendance improved once graded practice began.
options.d: A learning disorder is primary because incomplete work remains even after school avoidance and nurse use decrease.

sections.stem:
During the next seven weeks, Caleb and the counselor develop a visual fear ladder and practice brief coping responses. The caregivers and school implement a graded attendance plan, a consistent morning routine, a tablet cutoff, a classroom visual checklist, a brief arrival check-in, and a structured nurse protocol that includes criteria for medical reassessment.

Caleb’s attendance improves from approximately two days per week to four days per week. The time required to enter school decreases from about 60 minutes to 15 minutes. Nurse visits decrease from approximately four per week to one per week, and his anxiety score decreases.

No new medical or safety concerns emerge. Caleb now sleeps approximately nine and a half hours on most school nights.

The remaining absences cluster on mornings when repeated reassurance ends with permission to remain home. Caleb’s assignment completion, teacher-rated inattention, and caregiver-rated organizational problems remain impaired. Reading fluency also remains below the expected range.

The caregivers continue to disagree about how to respond to morning nausea.

The school requests Caleb’s full counseling record to help plan classroom supports. The current authorization permits communication for attendance and school-support coordination. Caleb and both caregivers agree that the counselor may share functional information and recommendations. Caleb asks that his drawings and detailed statements about family conflict not be provided to the school.

sections.title: SECTION 1 - INITIAL PRESENTATION
sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which inquiry would most directly clarify Renee’s current risk of suicide or violence?

options.a: Clarify the recent head impact, headache progression, disorientation episodes, sleep, medication use, changes from Renee’s usual baseline, and functioning.
options.b: Assess cannabis amount, potency, timing, tolerance, withdrawal, perceived sleep benefit, cognitive effects, driving, and interest in changing use.
options.c: Explore trauma reminders, nightmares, avoidance, guilt, military experiences, family strain, and what Renee believes the symptoms mean.
options.d: Assess current suicidal and violent thoughts, intent, plans, preparation, firearm access, past behavior, protective factors, and ability to collaborate.

questions.question_text: Which approach best represents an appropriate mental status examination at this point?

options.a: Observe for intoxication and postpone the remainder of the mental status examination until Renee has abstained from cannabis.
options.b: Administer a brief cognitive screen and treat an impaired score as evidence that the episodes are primarily neurological.
options.c: Reconstruct one zoning-out episode and classify it as dissociation when Renee identifies a trauma-related trigger before the event.
options.d: Assess appearance, behavior, orientation, attention, memory, speech, thought process, perception, insight, judgment, and change from Renee’s usual functioning.

questions.question_text: Which chronology would best help distinguish the leading explanations for Renee’s cognitive change?

options.a: Compare trauma reminders, physiological arousal, altered awareness, memory during each episode, recovery pattern, and avoidance across different settings afterward.
options.b: Build an integrated timeline of postdeployment baseline, recent head impact, symptom worsening, trauma cues, cannabis, sleep, driving events, and recovery.
options.c: Compare cannabis product, potency, timing, sleep, medications, episode onset, next-day functioning, and periods when Renee does not use.
options.d: Compare blast history, initial recovery, longstanding headaches, prior cognitive baseline, neurological follow-up, and functional changes consistently across settings over time.

questions.question_text: Which inquiry would provide the most clinically useful assessment of Renee’s cannabis use?

options.a: Clarify the benefits Renee attributes to cannabis, her treatment priorities, alternatives tried for sleep, and concerns about reducing use.
options.b: Compare symptoms on use and nonuse nights, then infer whether cannabis is therapeutic, harmful, or unrelated to the current presentation.
options.c: Assess product, potency, amount, timing, tolerance, withdrawal, unsuccessful cutbacks, impairment, driving effects, treatment goals, and readiness to change.
options.d: Review diagnostic criteria for cannabis use disorder, leaving cognition and driving questions for the medical and neurological evaluations.

sections.stem:
Renee is a 38-year-old military veteran. Nine years ago, she was near a blast during deployment. Since returning home, she has experienced nightmares, heightened startle, avoidance of certain reminders, intermittent headaches, and mild forgetfulness. Until recently, those cognitive symptoms had remained relatively stable, and she had continued working and caring for her 16-year-old son.

During the past 10 days, Renee’s headaches have become more persistent, and family members have noticed periods of confusion. Two weeks ago, she fell from a step stool and struck the back of her head. She did not seek medical evaluation.

Three times during the past week, Renee has “lost track” of what she was doing for approximately 20–60 seconds. While driving a familiar route, she briefly did not recognize where she was and drifted across the center line. Another driver’s horn alerted her, and she corrected the vehicle.

Renee uses a high-potency cannabis concentrate every night and sometimes takes a second dose after awakening. She says it is the only intervention that helps her sleep.

Renee keeps a loaded handgun in an unlocked bedside drawer. She says, “I would never use it on myself, but some nights I do not care whether I wake up.” During a recent argument, she yelled at her son and punched a wall.

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Which disposition is most proportionate to the information now available?

options.a: Continue outpatient counseling with daily contact, secure the firearm at home, suspend driving, and obtain medical evaluation within forty-eight hours.
options.b: Arrange voluntary psychiatric admission first, with neurological assessment occurring after the suicide and aggression risks have been stabilized.
options.c: Initiate involuntary psychiatric hospitalization because the prior attempt, loaded firearm, passive death wishes, and wall punching establish imminent danger.
options.d: Arrange same-day emergency medical evaluation, safe transportation, no driving, collaborative firearm restriction, and psychiatric risk reassessment during the handoff.

questions.question_text: Which concurrent-referral plan best supports coordinated care?

options.a: Define each referral question, obtain purpose-specific releases, arrange warm handoffs, clarify provider roles, and track whether recommended care occurs.
options.b: Refer to psychiatry as the central provider and ask that clinician to coordinate neurological, substance-related, sleep, and trauma concerns.
options.c: Provide separate referral options for each concern and ask Renee to update the counselor after she schedules the appointments.
options.d: Refer to neurology first and pause counseling until a medical provider determines whether trauma, cannabis, or sleep contributes to symptoms.

questions.question_text: Renee says, “Cannabis is the only reason I sleep. Every provider acts like it is the whole problem.” Which response best demonstrates empathic attunement?

options.a: Because sleep matters so much, we should avoid changing cannabis use until another intervention consistently produces the same benefit for you over time.
options.b: Cannabis has been one of the few ways you can get sleep. Could we examine what it helps and what it may complicate?
options.c: The medical team can determine whether cannabis affects cognition; our sessions can focus on trauma and the conflict with your son.
options.d: You have made your position clear, so I will not raise cannabis again unless you decide that it is a problem.

questions.question_text: Before choosing veteran-specific resources or adapting treatment, which approach BEST aligns care with Renee's population context?

options.a: Present VA, Vet Center, and community treatment options, then ask which setting best fits Renee's access, privacy, and trust preferences.
options.b: Explore how military service and prior care affect help-seeking, then ask whether veteran-specific treatment or community care feels more relevant to Renee.
options.c: Ask how service, deployment, gender, family role, trust, and prior care shape Renee's preferences, then adapt treatment to the elements she identifies.
options.d: Ask whether military culture contributes to reluctance about vulnerability and, if Renee agrees, incorporate psychoeducation about common veteran help-seeking barriers.

sections.stem:
Direct assessment reveals that Renee has passive thoughts about not waking up approximately two or three nights each week. She denies current active suicidal intent, a suicide plan, preparatory behavior, or recently handling the firearm while distressed. She reports one interrupted suicide attempt during deployment nine years ago.

Renee says the wall-punching incident occurred while her son was in another room. She did not threaten him, did not intend to harm him, and left the home briefly to cool down. She expresses concern and remorse about the effect of her behavior on him.

Renee is cooperative but guarded when cannabis is discussed. Her speech is clear, and her thought process is linear. She reports no hallucinations, fixed unusual beliefs, elevated mood, grandiosity, or reduced need for sleep. She is oriented to person and place but gives the date incorrectly by two days. She has difficulty sustaining attention and recalls only one of three words after a delay. She does not appear acutely intoxicated.

Renee explains that her intermittent headaches following deployment had been stable. Since the recent fall, the headaches have become persistent and more intense, and the episodes of disorientation are new.

She uses high-potency cannabis nightly, has gradually increased the amount needed for the same effect, experiences worse sleep and irritability when she skips it, and has made two unsuccessful attempts to reduce her use. She reports no other substance use.

A trusted friend can provide transportation and is legally able and willing to assist with temporary firearm storage. Renee agrees not to drive, to receive same-day medical evaluation, and to authorize purpose-specific coordination with medical and psychiatric providers.

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: Which information-sharing plan best matches the authorizations and recipient roles?

options.a: Ask Renee to communicate clinical details herself, while the counselor shares only appointment dates and attendance with every outside party.
options.b: Use separate authorizations: share safety-role information with the friend and purpose-relevant clinical information with each treating professional for coordination.
options.c: Use one authorization and provide the trusted friend and all treating professionals with the same summary and continuing clinical updates.
options.d: Release the complete counseling record to professional providers and give the friend verbal instructions for transportation and firearm storage.

questions.question_text: Which treatment-plan revision best addresses Renee’s request to begin trauma-focused work?

options.a: Begin a full trauma-focused protocol now because co-occurring cannabis use, sleep disturbance, and postconcussive symptoms do not necessarily contraindicate PTSD treatment.
options.b: Delay all trauma-focused treatment until Renee is symptom-free, abstinent from cannabis, medically discharged, and sleeping normally for several months.
options.c: Continue present-focused stabilization indefinitely because persistent disorientation and a history of blast exposure make trauma processing predictably unsafe.
options.d: Reassess medical change, orientation, participation capacity, risk, informed preference, and supports; then begin or adapt trauma-focused treatment when current safety permits.

questions.question_text: During a later session, Renee suddenly develops slurred speech, cannot identify where she is, and reports a sharply worsening headache. Which response is most appropriate?

options.a: Contact the trusted friend to monitor Renee overnight and arrange neurological follow-up the next morning if the symptoms continue.
options.b: Use grounding until Renee is oriented, end the trauma discussion, and arrange routine medical follow-up within the next twenty-four hours.
options.c: Explore the preceding trauma cue to determine whether dissociation explains the symptoms before deciding whether medical evaluation is necessary.
options.d: Pause treatment, reduce stimulation, assess immediate safety, activate emergency medical evaluation and safe transport, and confirm the handoff.

questions.question_text: After Renee develops the acute neurological change described in the case, which documentation BEST supports clinical continuity and later review?

options.a: Record onset and observed neurologic changes, MSE and risk findings, baseline comparison, emergency disposition, contacts and authority, handoff confirmation, unresolved questions, and follow-up.
options.b: Record current neurologic observations, client statements, emergency disposition and handoff, and reference the earlier risk and firearm note rather than reassessing current status.
options.c: Record observations, risk findings, emergency action, support contact, handoff, and follow-up while documenting a working impression of dissociation versus neurologic injury.
options.d: Record current observations, risk status, contacts, emergency disposition, handoff, and follow-up while omitting the disclosure authority because emergency care was clinically necessary.

questions.question_text: After Renee completes emergency evaluation and returns to coordinated outpatient care, which interpretation best reflects the treatment data to date?

options.a: The plan is producing broad improvement, so persistent cognitive episodes can be monitored without changing provider roles or treatment targets.
options.b: Safety, sleep, and family functioning are improving; persistent cognitive and PTSD symptoms require continued coordination and plan revision.
options.c: Cannabis reduction may be driving the gains, so hold trauma intervention until a longer abstinence trial clarifies symptom causality.
options.d: Safety has improved enough to close suicide monitoring, while trauma, sleep, cannabis, and cognitive care continue through separate providers.

sections.stem:
Renee completes same-day emergency medical and psychiatric evaluation. No acute intracranial emergency is identified, but further neurological and postconcussive follow-up is recommended. The psychiatric evaluation does not indicate inpatient admission under the current findings. Renee and the treatment team develop a collaborative safety plan with continued risk monitoring.

Her trusted friend arranges lawful temporary firearm storage outside Renee’s home. Renee does not have access to the firearm and agrees not to drive until medically cleared or while disorientation continues.

Four weeks later, Renee has experienced no passive death-related thoughts for three weeks and no further threats, wall punching, or other aggressive behavior. Sleep has improved from approximately three to four hours to five and a half to six hours most nights. She has reduced cannabis use from one or more doses every night to use on four or five nights each week.

Her headaches are less intense, but she has experienced two additional brief episodes of disorientation. Trauma-related nightmares, avoidance, and hyperarousal remain marked. Renee says, “I have handled the safety problems. I want to start trauma-focused treatment now.”

Renee has signed separate authorizations. Her friend may receive information needed to fulfill the agreed transportation, firearm-storage, and safety-support role. Medical, psychiatric, neurological, and substance-related providers may receive clinically relevant information needed for their respective treatment and coordination roles.

sections.title: SECTION 1 - INITIAL PRESENTATION
sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which assessment approach would provide the strongest foundation for the initial formulation?

options.a: Focus first on food intake, exercise, and weight history, adding psychiatric and social assessment after the eating pattern is clarified.
options.b: Map eating and weight changes, exercise, medical symptoms, mood and risk, substances, functioning, supports, and athletic pressures across time.
options.c: Begin with scholarship and team pressures, then assess eating behaviors only after Keisha explains how athletics affects her current distress.
options.d: Administer eating-disorder, anxiety, and depression measures first, then use the highest score to organize the remaining diagnostic interview.

questions.question_text: Keisha says, “If my coach thinks I am weak, I could lose everything. Running is the only thing I am really good at.” Which response best demonstrates empathic responding?

options.a: You are afraid that getting help could threaten the scholarship and the identity you have built around running. Tell me more.
options.b: I hear how important running is, and I can assure you that your coach will not learn anything unless you choose.
options.c: Your scholarship matters, but these physical symptoms mean health has to come before athletics even if that affects your season.
options.d: It sounds as though perfectionism is making running feel like your only strength. We should work on broadening your identity.

questions.question_text: Which inquiry BEST integrates cultural and contextual factors into Keisha's treatment?

options.a: Explore how sport culture and scholarship pressure shape restriction, then ask how family, cultural, and body-image experiences may add to or buffer those pressures.
options.b: Ask how sport norms, body ideals, scholarship pressure, family or cultural experience, and prior health care matter to Keisha without assuming which explains symptoms.
options.c: Ask which identity feels most threatened by treatment—athlete, student, or family or community member—and use that priority to guide early alliance work.
options.d: Explore structural pressures in collegiate athletics and how Keisha has navigated them before focusing on her personal beliefs about weight, rest, and performance.

sections.stem:
Keisha is a 20-year-old collegiate distance runner who receives a substantial athletic scholarship. She was referred for counseling because of increasing anxiety and perfectionism.

During the past seven months, Keisha has become increasingly restrictive with food. She routinely skips meals, avoids foods she considers “too heavy,” weighs herself several times a day, and adds unscheduled running or cross-training when she believes she has eaten too much.

Keisha has continued exercising despite a diagnosed stress fracture. She reports dizziness when standing, frequent fatigue, feeling cold, and four months without a menstrual period.

She says, “Everyone on the team talks about discipline. If I gain weight, I will slow down.” She worries that her coach may reduce her role or scholarship if others learn she is struggling.

Keisha says running has structured most of her life since middle school and adds, “If I am not a runner, I honestly do not know what I am good at.”

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Which provisional diagnosis is best supported by the information now available?

options.a: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, because Keisha restricts substantially and has developed significant medical and nutritional consequences.
options.b: Atypical anorexia nervosa, because the amount of weight loss and medical compromise are more important than her current body weight.
options.c: Anorexia nervosa, restricting type, because low weight, restriction, fear of weight gain, and weight-related overvaluation are all present.
options.d: Other specified feeding or eating disorder, because athletic training makes it difficult to determine whether low weight is clinically significant.

questions.question_text: Which level-of-care response is most appropriate at this point?

options.a: Continue outpatient counseling with daily check-ins while arranging sports-medicine and dietitian appointments within the next several days.
options.b: Refer directly to a residential eating-disorder program because her low weight and exercise behavior establish the need for twenty-four-hour behavioral containment.
options.c: Arrange psychiatric hospitalization because severe restriction, compulsive exercise, and scholarship fears indicate that Keisha cannot safely manage outpatient treatment.
options.d: Arrange immediate medical evaluation in a setting able to assess and stabilize eating-disorder-related physiological compromise before outpatient planning continues.

questions.question_text: What should the counselor do in response to Keisha’s acute dizziness and near-collapse?

options.a: Keep Keisha seated, offer fluids and a snack if she agrees, and reassess symptoms before deciding whether medical transport is necessary.
options.b: Stop routine counseling, protect Keisha from falling, activate emergency medical response and safe transport, and remain involved until the handoff occurs.
options.c: Ask Keisha to contact a trusted person for transportation, provided she feels steadier after resting and agrees not to drive herself.
options.d: Call the eating-disorder program for admission guidance while monitoring Keisha in the office and delaying transport until placement is confirmed.

questions.question_text: After immediate medical needs are addressed, which concurrent-care plan is most appropriate?

options.a: Refer to an eating-disorder therapist and dietitian, then suspend counseling until those specialists determine which psychological issues remain appropriate for CTA counseling.
options.b: Ask the medical physician to direct the entire treatment plan so nutrition, exercise, psychotherapy, and return-to-sport decisions remain clinically consistent.
options.c: Coordinate medical, nutritional, psychiatric, and counseling care with defined questions, releases, provider roles, and follow-up responsibilities for each discipline.
options.d: Give Keisha several specialty referrals and let her decide which providers communicate, because too much coordination may reduce her autonomy.

questions.question_text: The counselor has experience treating anxiety and perfectionism but no supervised specialty experience treating eating disorders in athletes. Which response is most appropriate?

options.a: Continue treating anxiety and perfectionism independently, while specialists manage eating behaviors and medical issues outside the counselor’s treatment plan.
options.b: Disclose the competence limits, obtain consultation or supervision, and continue only clearly appropriate counseling functions within a coordinated plan.
options.c: Transfer all counseling to an eating-disorder specialist, because limited specialty experience prevents the counselor from retaining any therapeutic role.
options.d: Use established eating-disorder treatment manuals with close outcome monitoring, seeking consultation only if Keisha fails to improve as expected.

sections.stem:
Further assessment shows that Keisha is 5 feet 6 inches tall and currently weighs 104 pounds. Six months ago, she weighed 121 pounds. Her current medical record lists a BMI of approximately 16.8.

Keisha says she is intensely afraid of gaining weight and believes that weighing more than she does now would make her slower and less disciplined. Her self-evaluation is strongly tied to weight, appearance, running performance, and whether she follows her food and exercise rules.

She reports no binge-eating episodes and denies self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse, or other purging behaviors. She frequently exercises beyond the training plan and sometimes hides the additional exercise.

Keisha denies current suicidal thoughts, self-harm, psychotic symptoms, or substance misuse. She lives alone off campus and does not have an established local primary-care clinician.

Earlier that morning, the athletic health clinic documented a resting heart rate of 42 beats per minute and blood pressure of 88/56 mmHg while supine. After standing, her heart rate increased to 76 and her blood pressure fell to 78/50. Keisha became markedly dizzy.

She left the clinic before physician evaluation because she did not want to miss class.

Near the end of the counseling appointment, Keisha stands, becomes pale, reports tunnel vision, and her knees begin to buckle. The counselor assists her back into the chair.

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: Which next-phase counseling goal should Keisha and the counselor MOST appropriately establish together while medical and return-to-sport decisions remain with the multidisciplinary team?

options.a: Within four weeks, Keisha will obtain medical clearance to resume running and begin a graded return-to-sport plan with the counselor.
options.b: Within four weeks, Keisha will complete every nutrition and activity recommendation without deviation and report increased confidence in recovery.
options.c: Within four weeks, Keisha will lower weight-gain fear before beginning identity work, using weekly anxiety ratings to determine readiness for that next phase.
options.d: Within four weeks, Keisha will practice three coping responses for body or rest distress and identify two nonperformance sources of identity or support.

questions.question_text: Which response would best facilitate Keisha’s motivation to continue recovery?

options.a: Review the medical risks of premature return to sport and ask Keisha to commit to the treatment plan until the team clears competition.
options.b: Ask Keisha to list the costs of restriction until she recognizes that continued eating-disorder behavior conflicts with her scholarship goals.
options.c: Reassure Keisha that recovery will probably improve her future performance so the temporary exercise restrictions feel more worthwhile and manageable.
options.d: Explore what running, health, school, and long-term athletic goals mean to Keisha, then connect one chosen recovery step to those values.

questions.question_text: How should the counselor respond to the coach’s request?

options.a: Decline all communication with athletics so Keisha’s confidentiality remains protected, while allowing her to relay any recommendations she chooses.
options.b: Send the coach a brief summary of diagnosis, treatment attendance, current weight trend, and expected return date because scholarship decisions affect care.
options.c: Clarify Keisha’s authorization and the coach’s purpose, then share only agreed functional information while directing medical clearance questions to qualified providers.
options.d: Provide the coach the counselor’s psychological readiness opinion, while withholding weight, diagnosis, and treatment details unless Keisha authorizes them separately.

questions.question_text: Which counseling strategy best stays within the counselor’s role while addressing Keisha’s remaining difficulties?

options.a: Develop an eating and training schedule with Keisha so she can practice flexibility without relying on the treatment team’s prescriptions.
options.b: Use counseling to challenge weight beliefs until Keisha accepts the team’s target weight, then begin work on perfectionism and identity flexibility.
options.c: Practice coping with body-image distress, perfectionistic thoughts, rest-related guilt, identity shifts, and support-seeking while keeping prescriptions within team roles.
options.d: Focus on nonathletic hobbies and relationships until running no longer defines Keisha’s self-worth, then revisit sport-related coping and performance concerns.

questions.question_text: Which pre/post measurement plan BEST evaluates change in the counseling targets while medical outcomes continue to be monitored by Keisha's treatment team?

options.a: Repeat the same eating-disorder and anxiety measures at planned intervals and compare them with baseline restriction, exercise urges, body distress, mood, functioning, and unsafe behavior.
options.b: Repeat the same symptom measure and use weight, vital signs, and medical clearance as the primary benchmark for judging whether counseling has produced meaningful change.
options.c: Select the most relevant symptom measure each week and compare current scores with clinical impressions so measurement can follow whichever problem is most active.
options.d: Repeat general anxiety and depression measures and use medical-team reports for eating-disorder-specific outcomes so the counselor does not duplicate specialty assessment.

sections.stem:
Keisha is medically hospitalized for stabilization and later steps down to specialized eating-disorder treatment involving medical, nutritional, psychiatric, and psychotherapy services.

Eight weeks later, her medical team reports that her heart rate and orthostatic findings have improved and she has experienced no additional near-syncope. Her stress fracture is still healing. She has not been cleared to resume running or competition; return-to-sport decisions remain with the appropriate medical and sports-health clinicians.

Keisha is eating more consistently and has stopped secret additional workouts for the past three weeks. She continues to experience significant fear of weight gain, guilt when resting, and urges to compensate after meals.

She says, “I know I am doing better physically, but everyone keeps talking like running is the enemy. I want my life back.”

Keisha worries that teammates will move ahead of her and that the coach may replace her. She also says she has begun to realize that most of her friendships, routines, and self-esteem have revolved around running.

The counselor is participating in the coordinated treatment plan under qualified consultation.

Keisha has authorized communication among her treatment providers. A separate authorization allows the athletic trainer to receive functional participation restrictions necessary to support her care. She has not authorized the counselor to disclose psychotherapy details directly to her coach.

The coach contacts the counselor and requests Keisha’s diagnosis, current weight, treatment progress, and an estimate of when she can compete again.

sections.title: SECTION 1 - INITIAL PRESENTATION
sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which assessment would most directly clarify the clinical significance of Mateo's recent cutting?

options.a: Review wound care, substance use, sleep, recent stress, access to the cutting method, and who was present afterward.
options.b: Clarify relationship triggers, abandonment fears, urgent-message patterns, provider interactions, and what usually happens after Mateo receives rapid reassurance.
options.c: Assess cutting intent, expected outcome, medical severity, suicidal thoughts or plans, means, history, intoxication, and protective factors.
options.d: Complete mood, trauma, bipolar, substance, identity, and personality-pattern history before deciding whether the current episode represents acute risk.

questions.question_text: Mateo says, “Cutting is what keeps me from doing something worse.” Which response best demonstrates empathic responding while preserving safety assessment?

options.a: It sounds like cutting gives temporary relief when the pressure spikes. I want to understand that relief and what ‘something worse’ means.
options.b: If cutting prevents a suicide attempt, we can treat it as a temporary coping strategy while we build safer alternatives together.
options.c: You are telling me the urge becomes intense quickly. Let's identify a distress-tolerance skill you can use instead next time.
options.d: The fact that cutting reduces pressure does not make it safe. We need to focus first on stopping the behavior and risk.

questions.question_text: Which working hypothesis would be most useful for understanding Mateo's urgent-message pattern at this stage?

options.a: The messaging primarily reflects poor respect for boundaries, so firmer consequences will likely reduce the behavior without further relational analysis.
options.b: The messaging is best understood as evidence of a personality disorder because it escalates whenever the counselor is not immediately available.
options.c: The messaging mainly signals inadequate coping skills, so skills training should begin before exploring how counselor responses affect the pattern.
options.d: Urgent contact may briefly regulate abandonment fear and shape a repeating counselor-client cycle; examine triggers, responses, relief, and later consequences.

sections.stem:
Mateo is a 26-year-old client who reports recurrent superficial cutting since his late teens. His most recent episode occurred two days ago after his partner did not respond to several messages for several hours.

Mateo used a razor to make several shallow cuts on his forearm. The bleeding stopped without medical treatment. He says he did not expect or intend to die and describes the purpose as “getting the pressure out of my body.”

He adds, “Cutting is what keeps me from doing something worse.”

Mateo becomes intensely distressed when someone important to him seems unavailable. He describes close relationships as “either everything or completely fake” and reports frequently moving from feeling extremely close to someone to believing the person does not care about him.

Similar patterns occur in counseling. After difficult sessions, Mateo sometimes sends several urgent messages. When the counselor replies quickly, he reports brief relief but often sends another message seeking additional contact or clarification. When a reply does not come quickly, Mateo may write that the counselor is abandoning him and threaten to quit treatment.

The counselor has not yet reached a personality-disorder diagnosis.

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Which provisional diagnosis is best supported by the longitudinal evidence?

options.a: Bipolar II disorder, because Mateo has intense mood shifts, impulsive behavior, irritability, changing self-image, and rapidly changing judgments of close relationships.
options.b: Posttraumatic stress disorder, because abandonment sensitivity, anger, self-injury, and relationship instability can develop after adverse interpersonal experiences across many settings.
options.c: Alcohol-induced mood disorder, because binge drinking occurs during some crises and may intensify impulsivity, anger, and self-harm urges.
options.d: Borderline personality disorder, provisional, because pervasive abandonment sensitivity, unstable relationships and identity, affective reactivity, emptiness, anger, and self-harm are present.

questions.question_text: Which treatment-planning approach best organizes Mateo's current priorities?

options.a: Prioritize suicidal and self-injurious behavior, then therapy-interfering patterns, while also addressing alcohol and broader quality-of-life problems within the structured plan.
options.b: Prioritize alcohol reduction first because intoxication increases risk, then address self-harm and relationship problems after several weeks of reduced use.
options.c: Prioritize relationship stability and abandonment fears first because these triggers drive the other symptoms and will reduce risk indirectly.
options.d: Begin skills training across emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness, and distress tolerance simultaneously, allowing Mateo to choose which target matters most each week.

questions.question_text: Following a cutting episode, which intervention would provide the most useful DBT-informed behavioral analysis?

options.a: Reconstruct the prompting event, vulnerabilities, thoughts, emotions, actions, consequences, and points where alternative skills could interrupt the sequence.
options.b: Teach a distress-tolerance strategy and ask Mateo to practice it daily before examining the details of the most recent episode.
options.c: Review the safety plan and rehearse crisis contacts so Mateo has a clearer response if the urge to cut returns.
options.d: Examine the belief that delayed replies mean abandonment and use cognitive restructuring to generate more balanced interpretations for future conflicts.

questions.question_text: Mateo says angrily, “Your communication policy proves that you will abandon me too.” Which response best demonstrates conflict tolerance and resolution?

options.a: Explain that the policy applies to every client, reassure Mateo that the counselor still cares, and redirect the conversation toward treatment goals.
options.b: Temporarily allow additional after-hours replies while trust develops, then return to the original communication policy once Mateo feels more secure.
options.c: Acknowledge that the limit felt like abandonment, invite Mateo's anger into the discussion, maintain the boundary, and examine what happened between them.
options.d: Postpone discussion of the policy until Mateo is less angry, using the current session to practice emotion-regulation skills instead.

questions.question_text: The counselor notices feeling pulled between answering Mateo immediately at all hours and avoiding his messages altogether. What is the best response to this reaction?

options.a: Transfer Mateo to another clinician because strong counselor reactions indicate that objectivity and therapeutic usefulness have already been compromised.
options.b: Tell Mateo that the volume of messages is exhausting so he can understand the effect his behavior has on the counselor.
options.c: Notice the pull toward overavailability or withdrawal, seek supervision or consultation, and use that awareness to maintain a consistent treatment frame.
options.d: Increase responsiveness temporarily to reduce the counselor's anxiety about risk, then tighten the boundary after Mateo becomes more stable.

sections.stem:
Further assessment shows that Mateo's relationship instability began in late adolescence and has occurred across romantic relationships, friendships, family relationships, and several treatment relationships.

He describes chronic feelings of emptiness and an unstable sense of who he is. His career plans, values, and view of himself can shift markedly depending on whether he feels accepted or rejected by someone important to him. During interpersonal conflict, he can move within hours from intense attachment to anger and rejection.

Mateo reports no distinct multiday periods of elevated or expansive mood, grandiosity, markedly increased goal-directed activity, or reduced need for sleep. He reports adverse childhood experiences but does not currently describe a trauma syndrome that accounts for the full longitudinal pattern.

Several times per month during severe interpersonal conflicts, Mateo drinks five to seven alcoholic beverages in an evening. Some cutting episodes have occurred after drinking, although the relationship and self-image patterns also occur when he is sober.

At age 19, Mateo intentionally took a large quantity of over-the-counter medication because he wanted to die. A roommate found him and called emergency services. Mateo received medical treatment.
