Currently, Mateo reports brief passive thoughts such as “I wish I could disappear” approximately once or twice per week. He denies a current suicide plan, intent, or preparatory behavior. He agrees to reduce access to excess medications and identifies his sister and one close friend as reliable supports.

The counselor reviews a written communication and crisis policy. Routine messages are generally answered during business hours, while urgent after-hours safety concerns are directed to designated crisis resources rather than guaranteed immediate counselor response.

Mateo becomes angry and says, “So when I actually need you, you're going to disappear. You're just like everyone else.”

He nevertheless agrees to continue discussing the treatment structure and begins a structured DBT-informed treatment plan.

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: What is the most appropriate professional response to Mateo's public social-media post?

options.a: Ignore the post entirely because responding clinically to public online content would violate Mateo's privacy, blur treatment boundaries, and reinforce online contact.
options.b: Avoid publicly confirming or disputing the counseling relationship, assess safety privately, document the clinical significance, and address the rupture through established channels.
options.c: Post a general statement that the practice cannot discuss current or former clients, without naming Mateo or addressing his specific complaint.
options.d: Send Mateo a private message through the platform asking him to remove the post, then discuss the conflict and safety at the next appointment.

questions.question_text: Which treatment-plan revision best addresses the pattern revealed by the counselor's vacation?

options.a: Prepare explicitly for future absences by identifying likely triggers, alternative supports, message expectations, crisis routes, skills, and a post-return session plan.
options.b: Increase counselor availability around future absences so Mateo experiences continuity, then gradually reduce extra contact after the relationship feels more secure.
options.c: Keep the current plan unchanged because modifying boundaries after a rupture may reinforce escalation and teach Mateo that crises alter treatment structure.
options.d: Pause absence-related work until Mateo has several weeks without self-harm urges, then revisit how planned separations affect the therapeutic relationship.

questions.question_text: Which response best facilitates awareness of the here-and-now therapeutic interaction?

options.a: I gave you advance notice and coverage information, so I want us to focus on how your interpretation of the vacation escalated the conflict.
options.b: I am sorry the vacation hurt you. I should have been more available, and I will try not to take extended time away again.
options.c: When I was unavailable, it felt like proof that I would leave. Can we look at what you expected, felt, and did between us?
options.d: The public post crossed an important boundary. Before discussing the vacation, we need to decide how you will repair the harm to the practice.

questions.question_text: Which interpretation best reflects Mateo's treatment progress to date?

options.a: Self-injury and skill use are improving, but rupture-linked urges, alcohol episodes, attendance problems, and suicide risk still require active monitoring.
options.b: Treatment is broadly successful because cutting has decreased substantially, so the remaining interpersonal and alcohol concerns can be handled during maintenance.
options.c: Treatment is ineffective because the vacation triggered renewed self-harm urges, missed sessions, and public criticism despite several weeks of earlier progress.
options.d: The reduction in cutting indicates lower suicide risk, so future monitoring can focus primarily on relationship functioning and treatment attendance.

questions.question_text: Which revision would produce the strongest ongoing safety plan?

options.a: List NSSI warning signs, distress-tolerance skills, supportive contacts, and office hours, while instructing Mateo to use emergency services for any suicidal thought.
options.b: Link warning signs, NSSI urges, shifts toward suicidal intent or planning, internal coping, supports, crisis routes, means safety, and clear escalation thresholds.
options.c: Focus the plan on suicidal intent, means restriction, and emergency services, while treating NSSI urges as a psychotherapy target rather than a safety-plan concern.
options.d: Use one after-hours clinician contact pathway for NSSI and suicidal crises so Mateo does not have to decide which level of risk is occurring.

sections.stem:
After approximately 10 weeks of structured treatment, Mateo's cutting decreases from roughly weekly to one episode during the past six weeks. He has made no suicide attempts. Passive suicidal thoughts occur less often, and he uses distress-tolerance or interpersonal skills before acting on urges more consistently.

Alcohol-related crises have decreased but have not disappeared. Mateo has had one binge-drinking episode during the past six weeks.

He generally attends scheduled sessions and has become more willing to discuss relationship ruptures rather than terminating treatment immediately.

The counselor then schedules a one-week vacation. Several weeks beforehand, the counselor tells Mateo the dates, reviews the usual communication limits, identifies crisis coverage and alternative supports, and discusses the possibility that the absence may be difficult.

During the vacation, Mateo sends multiple messages to the usual practice communication channel. He does not report a suicide plan or emergency in the messages. He also posts publicly on social media: “Therapists pretend they care until they leave you when you need them.” He tags the practice's professional account. The counselor becomes aware of the post because the practice receives the tag notification; the counselor had not searched Mateo's social-media account.

After the vacation, Mateo misses two appointments. When he returns, he reports intense urges to cut during the absence but says he did not act on them. He denies current active suicidal ideation, plan, intent, or preparation.

Mateo says, “If you actually cared, you would apologize publicly and tell people you left me when I needed you.”

sections.title: SECTION 1 - INITIAL PRESENTATION
sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which assessment approach would provide the STRONGEST foundation for the counselor’s initial formulation?

options.a: Center the interview on grief intensity, loss chronology, coping, spouse support, and family pressure, adding broader psychiatric assessment as indicated.
options.b: Center the interview on reproductive follow-up, sleep, and work functioning, then explore cultural and spiritual meanings after symptom severity is established.
options.c: Build a timeline integrating loss and medical course, grief, mood, trauma, safety, sleep, functioning, supports, avoidance, and spiritual or cultural meaning.
options.d: Begin with standardized grief, depression, trauma, and functioning measures, then direct the interview toward the domains showing greatest severity.

questions.question_text: Which additional pattern would MOST strongly support a co-occurring major depressive episode rather than grief-related distress alone?

options.a: Grief comes in waves around reminders, while connection with her spouse and interest in some activities remain available between waves.
options.b: Yearning and guilt remain focused on the loss, while functioning improves when Mei feels supported and less pressured by family.
options.c: Sleep worsens and social avoidance increases after repeated family questions, with distress easing when those interactions become less intense.
options.d: Depressed mood and loss of interest occur most days, generalized worthlessness develops, and impairment extends well beyond loss-related reminders.

questions.question_text: Mei asks, “Does karma mean this happened because I failed somehow?” Which counselor response is BEST?

options.a: Would you like me to consult a Buddhist teacher before we explore this further so that we do not misinterpret your tradition?
options.b: Would it help if we used Buddhist teachings on compassion to replace the punitive interpretation with a more supportive spiritual meaning?
options.c: What does karma or moral failure mean to you here, and when does your practice bring compassion versus self-blame?
options.d: Guilt is common after loss; let’s examine evidence for and against personal responsibility before deciding whether the belief has spiritual meaning.

questions.question_text: Which assessment would BEST determine whether a distinct trauma-related syndrome is also present?

options.a: Explore the course of grief waves, loss-focused reminders, avoidance, support, physiological distress, and how quickly symptoms settle after each trigger.
options.b: Clarify the medical and loss experience, then assess intrusion, avoidance, negative mood or cognition, arousal, dissociation, duration, and impairment.
options.c: Ask whether Mei describes the medical experience as traumatic and whether appointments now produce marked fear, physiological distress, or avoidance.
options.d: Use a validated trauma screener and prioritize trauma-focused treatment if the score is elevated while continuing to monitor grief.

sections.stem:
Mei is a 35-year-old Chinese American client who seeks counseling ten weeks after a pregnancy loss. She completed obstetric follow-up, and no current acute medical complication has been identified. Since the loss, sadness and guilt have tended to come in waves, particularly around medical appointments, pregnancy announcements, and gatherings involving friends’ infants. She sleeps five to six interrupted hours most nights and continues working part time. On less intense days, she can enjoy dinner or a walk with her spouse and feels emotionally connected to him. She has nevertheless declined several invitations from friends with infants.

Mei’s parents know that the pregnancy ended but do not know the detailed medical circumstances. They frequently urge her to “move on” and begin trying for another pregnancy. Mei says Buddhism has been meaningful to her for many years. She explains, “Part of me keeps thinking I did something wrong and this is karma, but I’m not even sure that’s what I believe. Sometimes my practice feels compassionate; sometimes I use it to punish myself.” She denies current suicidal ideation, any past suicide attempt, and any history of self-injury.

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Which counseling plan is BEST matched to Mei’s current presentation?

options.a: Use grief-informed counseling that combines meaning-making, paced approach to avoided reminders, restoration activities, and spiritual resources chosen by Mei.
options.b: Use trauma-focused exposure around medical reminders because avoidance is present, while monitoring grief reactions as a separate treatment target.
options.c: Use supportive counseling and an early family session to reduce pressure, adding individual grief work after parent communication becomes more stable.
options.d: Emphasize behavioral activation and restoration activities, postponing direct loss-focused work until sleep and daily routines become more consistent.

questions.question_text: Before the counselor communicates with Mei’s parents, which step is BEST?

options.a: Clarify whether Mei wants rehearsal or direct contact; if contact is chosen, agree on recipients, purpose, specific content, limits, risks, and authorization first.
options.b: Send a brief boundary statement now because Mei initially requested help, then document her verbal permission and preferred limits at the next session.
options.c: Obtain a broad written release for both parents so the counselor can adjust what is discussed as questions arise during the conversation.
options.d: Recommend that Mei speak with her parents herself first, reserving counselor contact for later if family pressure continues despite her efforts.

questions.question_text: Mei wants to remain close to her parents while protecting privacy around grief and reproductive decisions. Which counselor response BEST demonstrates respect for diversity?

options.a: Explore whether temporary distance from Mei's parents would create needed space while preserving ordinary family contact if that remains important to her.
options.b: Ask which parts of family responsibility Mei wants to preserve and which expectations feel burdensome, then consider whether her parents' intentions change the boundary she wants.
options.c: Explore whether direct or indirect boundary styles better fit Mei's family and choose the approach most likely to reduce conflict while preserving closeness.
options.d: Ask what privacy and family connection each mean to Mei, then help her construct a boundary consistent with both without privileging independence or compliance.

questions.question_text: Which intervention BEST incorporates cultural considerations into Mei's family-boundary work?

options.a: Use family-of-origin exploration to identify intergenerational loss and communication patterns, then apply whichever themes Mei identifies as relevant to the current family conflict.
options.b: Broach bicultural experience and filial expectations, focusing on how they affect communication with Mei's parents about pregnancy loss and future decisions.
options.c: Explore whether traditional, contemporary, family-specific, or personal values best describe the tension, then use that language when practicing boundaries with her parents.
options.d: Explore how bicultural identity, filial responsibility, privacy, generational roles, and family experience interact for Mei, then adapt communication practice to her preferred balance.

sections.stem:
Further assessment shows that Mei does not have pervasive anhedonia or generalized worthlessness. Between grief waves she can enjoy time with her spouse and occasionally with friends. She reports no history of mania or psychosis, no current substance misuse, and no suicidal ideation.

Mei vividly remembers receiving the news about the pregnancy loss and sometimes cries before medical appointments. She does not report recurrent flashbacks, trauma-related nightmares, persistent hypervigilance, or a broader pattern of trauma symptoms. Her spouse remains supportive.

Her parents continue to call frequently. Mei says maintaining a close relationship with them is important and that she feels a strong responsibility not to make them worry. She also wants privacy and control over reproductive decisions. She initially says, “Could you tell them to stop asking when we’re trying again?” She then pauses and adds, “Actually, I don’t know if I want you talking to them. I want help figuring out how to handle it.”

Mei describes meditation and compassion practices as personally meaningful and says she may want to create a remembrance ritual if she can design something that feels authentic to her rather than something prescribed by someone else.

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: During a progress review, which summary BEST reflects Mei's treatment trajectory?

options.a: The current goals are not being met because the due-date reaction shows Mei is still unable to tolerate major grief reminders without significant symptom recurrence.
options.b: Overall goals show progress in sleep, social engagement, boundaries, and functioning; review the due-date flare as meaningful data without treating it automatically as failure.
options.c: The goals are essentially complete because Mei maintained work, relationships, and safety while the due-date symptoms began easing without major intervention.
options.d: Progress cannot be reviewed accurately until the due-date symptoms fully resolve because temporary grief intensification makes current functioning difficult to interpret.

questions.question_text: Which interpretation BEST reflects the available evidence about counseling effectiveness?

options.a: Treatment is not working because grief intensity increased despite several months of counseling and renewed social engagement.
options.b: Treatment is complete because work, relationships, and social activity improved despite temporary distress around the expected due date.
options.c: Overall functioning and coping have improved, while the time-limited trigger-related increase remains meaningful outcome data that requires continued monitoring.
options.d: Improvement cannot be attributed to counseling because spouse support and changes in family pressure occurred during the same period.

questions.question_text: How should the counselor respond to Mei’s mother’s new questions?

options.a: Share only information within the current authorization, decline the new diagnosis, prognosis, and reproductive-readiness questions, and revisit any expanded disclosure with Mei.
options.b: Provide general diagnostic and prognosis information because Mei’s mother already knows about the loss and the counselor has limited family authorization.
options.c: Decline all further family communication because the mother requested information beyond the current authorization and therefore invalidated the earlier permission.
options.d: Answer prognosis questions but not diagnosis or medical details, because general recovery expectations may help the parents reduce pressure without revealing private facts.

questions.question_text: Mei now says, “I don’t know whether I want another pregnancy or whether I just feel that I should.” Which strategy would BEST support her decision-making?

options.a: Use cognitive restructuring to resolve the belief that the loss was karmic punishment before discussing any future reproductive choice.
options.b: Use a decisional balance comparing another pregnancy soon with delaying it, giving greater weight to practical consequences than to grief-related emotions.
options.c: Use values clarification to separate Mei’s own hopes about family, spirituality, health, and timing from guilt, perceived duty, and external expectations.
options.d: Use a family-of-origin map to identify inherited expectations, then prioritize choices most likely to preserve family harmony while reducing conflict.

questions.question_text: Which follow-up action is MOST appropriate?

options.a: Reopen weekly counseling prophylactically because recurring grief waves after discharge indicate that the previous gains are not yet durable without professional support.
options.b: Confirm that Mei remains free of major impairment and close the case permanently if she continues working and using social supports.
options.c: Focus the follow-up on whether Mei has decided about another pregnancy because reproductive planning is the main unresolved issue from the prior treatment.
options.d: Review functioning, triggers, coping and support use, any new risk or diagnostic change, and whether booster care or reproductive supports are desired.

sections.stem:
During the next four months, Mei creates a private remembrance ritual of her own design. She resumes weekly walks with a friend and attends several social gatherings she previously would have avoided. Her sleep increases to about seven hours most nights, and she maintains her usual part-time work schedule.

Mei tells her parents, “I’ll bring up future pregnancy if and when I’m ready.” They ask less often, and Mei reports that the relationship remains important to her. After discussing the decision carefully, Mei authorizes the counselor to communicate one limited message to her parents: Mei wants the family to allow her to decide when or whether to discuss another pregnancy, and she appreciates their continued ordinary contact. Mei does not authorize disclosure of her diagnosis, medical details, prognosis, or treatment content.

As the expected due date arrives, Mei experiences eight to ten days of increased crying and interrupted sleep and declines a baby shower. She continues working, spends time with her spouse, uses her remembrance ritual and social supports, and denies suicidal ideation. The intensity has begun easing by the next session. Mei says, “Maybe therapy failed if I can still feel this bad.”

Later that week, Mei’s mother emails the counselor asking for Mei’s diagnosis, how long the grief will last, and whether Mei is “ready to try again.”

sections.title: SECTION 1 - INITIAL PRESENTATION
sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which orientation framework BEST establishes group privacy and outside-contact expectations before sessions begin?

options.a: Explain the counselor's confidentiality duties, require binding member confidentiality pledges, and allow outside contact if members agree not to discuss group material.
options.b: Explain that members control their own behavior, let overlapping pairs set private rules, and use the general informed-consent agreement to cover social-media contact.
options.c: Review counselor and member confidentiality limits, prohibit members from acknowledging one another publicly, and address unavoidable workplace or neighborhood contact as individual exceptions.
options.d: Distinguish counselor confidentiality from member behavior, set shared privacy and outside-contact expectations, address social media explicitly, and explain that secrecy cannot be guaranteed.

questions.question_text: Before deciding whether Asha and Ben should participate in the same group, what should Alan do?

options.a: Exclude the employee with greater workplace authority so the lower-power employee can participate without concern about job consequences or inhibited disclosure.
options.b: Admit both employees after an enhanced confidentiality agreement and monitor whether their workplace relationship begins affecting participation once the group starts.
options.c: Assess voluntariness, likely inhibition, workplace power, privacy concerns, treatment goals, and realistic alternatives with each employee before deciding group placement.
options.d: Ask the two employees to decide together whether they can participate comfortably, then honor their decision if both understand confidentiality limitations.

questions.question_text: Which working hypothesis about Ben’s behavior is MOST appropriate to test?

options.a: Ben’s brief responses may reflect broader social anxiety rather than workplace power, so increase direct invitations before reconsidering whether the group is appropriate.
options.b: Workplace hierarchy may be suppressing Ben’s disclosure; test that hypothesis through observation and private check-in rather than assuming the meaning of his restraint.
options.c: Asha’s greater participation may be creating an airtime imbalance, so equalize speaking opportunities before exploring whether their workplace roles are clinically relevant.
options.d: Both employees may be protecting workplace information from the group, so establish a no-workplace-content agreement before interpreting the pattern further.

questions.question_text: Which plan BEST addresses members’ potential interactions outside the group?

options.a: Ask members never to acknowledge one another outside group, including in unavoidable workplace and neighborhood settings, unless both people explicitly agree first.
options.b: Establish shared expectations for accidental encounters, online contact, privacy, and voluntary social contact while acknowledging unavoidable overlaps and revisiting their effects.
options.c: Let each overlapping pair establish its own outside-contact rules privately so Alan does not impose one standard on different relationships.
options.d: Prohibit social-media connections among members and require disclosure to Alan whenever two members communicate outside group about one another.

sections.stem:
Alan is a 45-year-old counselor preparing to facilitate a 10-week closed outpatient group for eight adults with anxiety. The group combines anxiety-management work with interpersonal practice and discussion. Members are expected to attend weekly 90-minute sessions.

During screening, Alan learns that two prospective members, Asha and Ben, work at the same hospital. Asha is not Ben’s direct supervisor, but she occasionally provides input about his schedule requests and annual performance review. Ben says he wants the group but is unsure whether he could discuss workplace anxiety openly with Asha present. Asha says she believes she can keep the two roles separate.

Another prospective member, Nora, recognizes Leila from a neighborhood association. Nora and Leila report only occasional community contact and no current conflict.

At a pre-group orientation meeting, Ben participates freely when discussing general anxiety but becomes noticeably brief when workplace examples arise and glances toward Asha before answering. Alan observes the change without drawing a conclusion.

Several prospective members ask whether Alan can guarantee that nothing discussed in the group will ever be repeated outside it.

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Which intervention BEST fits the group’s current developmental needs?

options.a: Continue the planned anxiety curriculum while meeting individually with the affected members, then return to the incident only if attendance continues declining further.
options.b: Suspend Maya from the next session while trust recovers, then reconsider participation after an individual accountability and readiness meeting.
options.c: Ask members to vote on whether Maya should remain, using the decision to restore shared ownership of the group’s safety expectations.
options.d: Pause planned content to address the rupture, clarify impact and agreements, assess safety and fit, and help the early group rebuild working norms.

questions.question_text: Three members begin attacking Maya while two defend her and quieter members withdraw. Which response BEST uses linking and blocking?

options.a: Let the members who feel harmed complete their feedback first, then invite Maya and her supporters to respond after everyone has been heard.
options.b: Stop personal attacks, link different reactions to shared concerns about trust and exposure, and invite concise first-person responses from quieter members.
options.c: Invite Maya to answer each concern individually while Alan monitors tone and reminds members to keep their comments specific and respectful.
options.d: Stop discussion of Maya’s behavior and redirect members to their own feelings about trust so the group does not become punitive.

questions.question_text: After Alan interrupts the personal attacks, which intervention BEST fosters therapeutic group factors?

options.a: Invite members to describe their own reactions and needs, notice shared vulnerability, support accountability, and identify what would permit continued participation without requiring forgiveness.
options.b: Summarize the group’s common rules and ask every member to recommit to them so cohesion can reform around a shared behavioral standard before proceeding.
options.c: Ask Maya and Leila to conduct a structured repair dialogue in front of the group so members can learn from direct interpersonal resolution.
options.d: Normalize that early groups often encounter conflict and reassure members that working through the rupture can strengthen cohesion over time.

questions.question_text: Alan notices a strong urge to remove Maya immediately to protect Leila, followed by irritation when Maya becomes defensive. What should Alan do with this reaction?

options.a: Follow the protective impulse by suspending Maya now, then use consultation before deciding whether she can return to the group.
options.b: Tell the group that Alan feels protective of Leila and irritated with Maya so members understand why he is slowing the decision.
options.c: Counterbalance the protective reaction by giving Maya additional time to explain herself and ensuring her perspective receives equal group attention.
options.d: Notice the competing pulls, seek consultation or supervision, examine how they may shape judgment, and return to explicit safety and group-fit criteria.

sections.stem:
The group begins with eight members. During the first three sessions, participation increases gradually and members begin taking more interpersonal risks.

After the third session, Maya posts publicly on social media: “Someone in my anxiety group lies about panic attacks to get attention.”

The post does not name Leila, Alan, the practice, or the group. However, another member who follows Maya believes the post refers to Leila because Leila recently discussed feeling dismissed when others questioned whether her panic symptoms were genuine. That member sends Leila a screenshot.

Leila tells Alan that she feels exposed and is now afraid that people in her community could identify her. Maya says she was angry after the previous session and was “venting,” but insists that she never named anyone. She voluntarily deletes the post after Alan speaks with her.

There have been no threats, stalking, doxxing, or reports of intent to harm anyone.

At the next group meeting, three members begin criticizing Maya and saying she should leave. Two defend her. Several quieter members stop participating. Attendance at the following meeting drops from eight members to six.

The group is still early in its development, and Alan had planned to continue anxiety-management and interpersonal-practice content.

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: Which approach BEST manages Nora's planned departure from the group?

options.a: Share Nora's authorized statement at the next session, invite brief reactions, and then redirect to planned content so the departure does not dominate group work.
options.b: Offer Nora an optional closing session; if she declines, tell the group she transferred and address logistics without inviting discussion of private reasons.
options.c: Invite the group to process its assumptions about the departure before sharing Nora's authorized statement, then correct only information she permitted Alan to clarify.
options.d: With Nora's agreement, offer a closing opportunity or authorized statement, clarify transition logistics, and invite members to process the departure without adding private reasons.

questions.question_text: Which pre/post approach BEST determines whether the group's repair efforts are improving group functioning?

options.a: Compare attendance before and after repair and use individual anxiety-symptom change as the secondary indicator of whether the group has returned to effective functioning.
options.b: Repeat the psychological-safety rating after each session and treat return to the preincident mean as the primary evidence that the rupture has resolved.
options.c: Repeat the same safety or cohesion measure at planned intervals from the pre-rupture baseline and pair it with participation, attendance, and individual anxiety-function data.
options.d: Use open-ended member feedback after repair and compare themes with Alan's pre-rupture process notes so outcome assessment remains individualized rather than score-driven.

questions.question_text: How should Alan respond to Asha’s and Ben’s requests for individual therapy?

options.a: Accept one employee for individual therapy and refer the other, reducing overlapping roles while preserving access to a clinician already familiar with the group.
options.b: Before accepting, assess role-change consequences, workplace power, confidentiality conflicts, group impact, alternatives, and consultation; use separate referrals if conflicts cannot be managed.
options.c: Decline both requests because a group counselor should not provide individual therapy to any current group member regardless of circumstances or informed consent.
options.d: Accept both requests with separate informed-consent agreements, keeping individual-session information outside group and reviewing role conflicts only if problems later emerge.

questions.question_text: A member says, “I still don’t know what is actually safe to say here.” Which response BEST uses the here-and-now group process?

options.a: Invite members to notice what is happening now—what they are holding back, what feels risky, and what responses would increase workable trust.
options.b: Review the confidentiality agreement and acknowledge that no rule can eliminate all risk, then return to planned anxiety content after answering questions.
options.c: Ask members privately after group what feels unsafe, then summarize themes anonymously next session so concerns can be addressed without public pressure.
options.d: Ask members to identify specific rule changes that would make disclosure feel safe enough, then resume process work after the new agreement is adopted.

questions.question_text: Members ask Alan whether Nora left because of the social-media incident. Which response BEST respects Nora’s authorization?

options.a: Tell the group Nora left because privacy concerns remained, without mentioning the neighborhood connection or any other details from her private conversation.
options.b: Say Nora requested another treatment format and will continue elsewhere, then decline further questions because the exact reason remains confidential.
options.c: Use only Nora’s authorized statement, decline to confirm or deny specific reasons, and invite the group to process reactions to the departure.
options.d: Decline to discuss Nora’s departure at all once she leaves, even though she authorized a limited statement about changing treatment.

sections.stem:
During the next three sessions, Alan reviews the group agreement, facilitates structured discussion of the impact of the post, and conducts individual check-ins when clinically indicated. Maya acknowledges that the post had an effect she did not anticipate and reiterates that she deleted it. Leila resumes participating but remains more cautious than before the incident.

Attendance returns to seven of eight members. Anonymous weekly ratings of psychological safety, which fell sharply after the incident, improve but have not returned completely to their pre-incident level. No additional outside-group incidents are reported, and members continue making progress on individual anxiety goals.

Nora decides the group is no longer the right treatment setting for her and accepts a referral to another service. She authorizes Alan to tell the group only: “I decided this group is not the right fit for me and am moving to another treatment option.” She does not authorize Alan to explain her private reasons.

Asha and Ben remain in the group. Each separately asks Alan whether he can also become their individual therapist while they continue attending the group. Both say they trust Alan and would prefer not to begin again with another clinician.

During the next group meeting, another member says: “I’m participating again, but I still don’t know what is actually safe to say here.”

sections.title: SECTION 1 - INITIAL PRESENTATION
sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which inquiry would MOST directly clarify the immediate safety concerns in Harold's presentation?

options.a: Clarify Harold's depression, anxiety, cognition, sleep, alcohol use, medical conditions, medications, and recent changes in his own daily functioning.
options.b: Assess caregiver burden, marital role expectations, family supports, barriers to asking for help, respite access, and the recent increase in anger.
options.c: Review the spouse's dementia course, wandering history, medication and bathing needs, home hazards, backup care, and current level of supervision.
options.d: Clarify what “never coming back” means, suicidal or violent thoughts, recent caregiving lapses, current supervision, and Harold's ability to maintain safety.

questions.question_text: Harold says, “If I ask my kids for help, I've failed my spouse.” Which response BEST demonstrates empathic responding?

options.a: You have carried a great deal because caring for your spouse matters to you. Let's identify which tasks your children could take over.
options.b: Being a good husband seems deeply important to you, and asking for help feels like failing that commitment. What makes it mean failure?
options.c: You sound exhausted, but the current arrangement may be unsafe. We should separate the feeling of failure from the practical care decisions.
options.d: Many devoted spouses eventually need help. Accepting support does not mean you have failed, and your children may want to contribute.

questions.question_text: Which assessment plan would BEST permit the counselor to formulate both the severity of Harold's alcohol use and its relationship to caregiving safety?

options.a: Clarify amount, frequency, sleep-related use, medication interactions, caregiving-time drinking, and whether safety incidents followed alcohol use so immediate risk can be estimated.
options.b: Clarify tolerance, withdrawal, craving, unsuccessful cut-downs, consequences, prior alcohol history, and readiness for change so disorder severity can be estimated.
options.c: Clarify perceived benefits, concerns, prior change attempts, family feedback, and caregiving functioning on drinking versus nondrinking days so motivation can be explored.
options.d: Map amount, frequency, timing, tolerance, withdrawal, cut-down attempts, caregiving-time use, consequences, interactions, and function so both severity and safety can be formulated.

sections.stem:
Harold is 71 and is the primary caregiver for his spouse, who has moderate dementia. His spouse needs assistance with medications and bathing and has previously attempted to leave the home when confused. No other caregiver is regularly present.

Harold says he is exhausted and increasingly irritable. During the intake he says, “Sometimes I think about walking away and never coming back.”

Harold acknowledges leaving his spouse alone for two to three hours at a time when he runs errands, even though he worries about wandering. A neighbor is staying with his spouse during today's appointment.

Harold says he has also been “pouring more whiskey at night to shut my brain off,” but he has not yet described how much he drinks.

His two adult children live within an hour of the home. Harold has told them very little about how difficult caregiving has become. He says, “I promised I would take care of my spouse. If I ask my kids to step in, I've failed as a husband.”

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Which response BEST applies the legal rule supplied in the case?

options.a: Keep the information confidential if Harold immediately accepts respite and a supervision plan, reserving a report for any subsequent caregiving incident.
options.b: Ask the adult children to verify the medication, meal, and wandering events before deciding whether reasonable suspicion exists under the stated rule.
options.c: Coordinate dementia and respite services first, because exhaustion rather than malicious intent is driving the caregiving lapses described in the case.
options.d: Explain the stated duty, make the required protective report, share information necessary for that purpose, address immediate safety, and continue engaging Harold.

questions.question_text: After immediate protective steps are addressed, which concurrent-care plan BEST fits the household's needs?

options.a: Coordinate Harold's medical, sleep, and alcohol evaluation with dementia-care, respite, and home-safety services, defining roles, releases, handoffs, and follow-up responsibilities.
options.b: Ask the spouse's dementia clinician to coordinate the whole household plan so medication, supervision, Harold's sleep, alcohol, and counseling stay under one lead provider.
options.c: Refer Harold for alcohol treatment and the spouse for dementia services, then resume caregiver counseling after both specialty plans have been established.
options.d: Give Harold several medical, respite, and aging-service options and let him decide which providers communicate so his autonomy remains central.

questions.question_text: Which approach BEST helps Harold develop a sustainable support system?

options.a: Ask each adult child to take one fixed caregiving shift weekly, then use community respite only for duties the family cannot cover consistently each month.
options.b: Identify willing family, friends, and community resources, clarify each person's actual capacity, and build an agreed backup plan that does not depend on one caregiver.
options.c: Use professional respite and adult-day services instead of family help so Harold's children are not pulled into the marital caregiving relationship.
options.d: Ask Harold which child is most dependable, then invite that person to coordinate the family schedule and distribute responsibilities to other relatives.

questions.question_text: Harold says, “You betrayed me by reporting this.” Which response BEST demonstrates conflict tolerance and resolution?

options.a: I hear how angry you are. Before we discuss trust, I want us to review the safety events and why the report was necessary under the stated rule.
options.b: I understand this felt like a betrayal. I was required to act under the rule we discussed, and I want to understand what this did to our trust.
options.c: I am sorry the report damaged our relationship. Going forward, I will limit outside contact unless there is clear proof that immediate harm is occurring.
options.d: Your anger makes sense. If you no longer trust me after the report, we should discuss whether another counselor could work with you more effectively.

questions.question_text: Which formulation BEST captures a systemic pattern contributing to Harold's isolation?

options.a: Harold's overresponsibility and secrecy reduce opportunities for planned help, so support often appears only during crises and reinforces his sense of failure.
options.b: Harold's marital identity makes accepting help difficult, so changing his beliefs about independence should precede attempts to alter the family system.
options.c: The spouse's dementia is the central driver of the family pattern, so modifying caregiving demands should resolve most secrecy and relational tension.
options.d: The adult children's limited involvement has caused Harold's burnout, so family treatment should focus first on increasing their caregiving responsibility.

sections.stem:
Harold explains that “walking away and never coming back” means imagining getting in his car and leaving the caregiving situation. He denies wanting to die, current suicidal ideation, a suicide plan, previous suicide attempts, or thoughts or intent to physically harm his spouse.

He reports sleeping approximately three hours most nights.

During the past month, Harold has been drinking three to four standard alcoholic drinks on most evenings, compared with approximately one drink previously. He sometimes begins drinking before his spouse is settled for the night. He reports needing more alcohol than before to obtain the same relaxing effect and has twice tried to reduce his use but returned to the previous amount because he could not sleep.

Harold reports that he has missed three evening medication doses for his spouse during the past month. On one occasion, after becoming angry during an argument, he chose not to prepare the evening meal that his spouse depends on him to provide. A neighbor later brought food.

One week ago, Harold fell asleep and his spouse wandered outside during the night. A neighbor found his spouse several houses away and returned them home.

The spouse's dementia clinician has documented that the spouse currently requires reliable supervision because of wandering risk and assistance with medication management. Harold's adult children were unaware of the extent of the recent problems.

CASE LEGAL ASSUMPTION — FOR THIS SIMULATION ONLY: Assume Harold's jurisdiction requires a licensed counselor who, in professional practice, knows or reasonably suspects that a protected adult with substantial cognitive impairment has been neglected by a caregiver to make an immediate report to the designated protective-services agency. Reasonable suspicion is sufficient; proof and malicious intent are not required. The counselor may disclose information reasonably necessary to make the required report.

This is a fictional examination rule supplied for this case. Candidates are not expected to infer any particular state's reporting statute.

When the counselor explains the required protective response, Harold becomes angry and says, “I told you because I trusted you. Now you've betrayed me.”

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: Which treatment-plan revision BEST fits the current course?

options.a: Keep the existing plan unchanged until Harold's caregiver burden reaches the mild range, then decide whether additional family or substance-focused work is needed.
options.b: Shift primarily to relapse prevention because the report, respite plan, and absence of new neglect events show that the acute treatment targets are resolved.
options.c: Consolidate the safer supervision plan while revising targets for Harold's sleep, alcohol use, anger, support use, and changing caregiving demands.
options.d: Make family-repair sessions the primary treatment focus because practical supervision is now stable and Harold's remaining distress centers on his children's reactions.

questions.question_text: Which family-meeting structure BEST supports conflict resolution?

options.a: Ask Harold to explain the incidents and apologize first, then ask the children what caregiving help they are willing to provide after hearing his account.
options.b: Ask the children to divide medication, meal, and respite duties based on availability, while Harold retains overnight care and final household decision-making.
options.c: Set shared safety and relationship goals, invite each adult to state capacity and limits, negotiate voluntary roles, and create direct communication and backup procedures.
options.d: Keep the meeting focused on feelings and relationship repair, postponing practical role decisions until resentment and shame have decreased for everyone.

questions.question_text: Which response would BEST facilitate Harold's motivation to continue accepting support?

options.a: Review the decrease in safety incidents and explain that respite is working, then ask Harold to commit to keeping the current schedule for another month for now.
options.b: Explore the kind of spouse and father Harold wants to be, how the current arrangement fits those values, and which one support step he will choose next.
options.c: Ask Harold to list the costs of refusing help and compare them with the benefits of respite until he identifies enough reasons to continue.
options.d: Reassure Harold that accepting respite does not represent failure, then help him identify the family member or service he trusts most to take over care.

questions.question_text: When the counselor and Harold review treatment progress together, which summary BEST supports the next-phase discussion?

options.a: The main safety goals are met because there have been no new neglect events; Harold can step down while sleep and alcohol concerns continue through medical follow-up.
options.b: Progress remains insufficient because Harold still needs respite and uses alcohol; maintain the same counseling intensity until both concerns are fully resolved and family strain improves.
options.c: Counseling progress cannot be separated from the effects of respite and family support, so postpone judging goals until external services have been stable longer.
options.d: Household safety and support have improved, while sleep, alcohol use, help-seeking, and relationship strain remain active; review with Harold which goals feel met and what comes next.

questions.question_text: Which maintenance plan BEST prepares Harold for future caregiving changes?

options.a: Continue scheduled counseling while Harold remains the primary caregiver, because progressive dementia creates ongoing stress that cannot be managed through maintenance planning alone right now.
options.b: Plan around current respite and family arrangements, revising the plan only if the spouse's dementia progresses enough to require a different living setting.
options.c: Step down once the household has remained incident-free for several months, asking Harold to return if caregiver burden again reaches a severe level.
options.d: Link overload warning signs to backup care, respite, Harold's health and alcohol follow-up, family or community supports, reassessment, and changes in the spouse's care needs.

sections.stem:
Six weeks later, Harold's spouse has a structured supervision plan that includes professional respite, an adult-day program, and identified backup contacts. The spouse has had no further unsupervised wandering, missed medication doses, or missed meals.

Harold now sleeps approximately five and a half hours on most nights. After medical assessment and discussion of his alcohol use, he reports drinking one to two drinks on approximately three evenings per week rather than three to four drinks most nights. Alcohol use remains an active treatment and medical-monitoring issue.

One adult child helps coordinate appointments and groceries. The other can provide an occasional weekend visit but is not able to provide routine hands-on care. Neither child can provide overnight caregiving.

Harold initially resisted respite but now says the breaks help. He remains uncomfortable asking for assistance and says, “I still hate that people know I couldn't handle it.”

His relationship with his children is strained. Harold wants a family meeting because he worries they now see him as “a terrible person.” The children agree to attend but state that they cannot become full-time caregivers.

Harold's spouse continues to have moderate dementia with intermittent nighttime wakefulness, and the dementia-care team has explained that care requirements will need ongoing reassessment as the condition changes.

sections.title: SECTION 1 - INITIAL PRESENTATION
sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which assessment approach would provide the STRONGEST foundation for the counselor’s initial formulation?

options.a: Focus first on panic phenomenology and medical contributors, then address workplace and career factors after the broader anxiety pattern is clinically clearer.
options.b: Build an integrated timeline of panic episodes, triggers, medical and safety factors, workplace events, functioning, supports, constraints, and Fatima’s own cultural meanings.
options.c: Focus first on the workplace comments and legal or career goals, then assess panic only if symptoms continue to impair overall functioning.
options.d: Administer standardized anxiety and discrimination measures first, then let the highest symptom score determine which areas receive more detailed clinical follow-up.

questions.question_text: Fatima says, “Maybe I’m just being too sensitive.” Which counselor response BEST demonstrates empathic responding at this point?

options.a: We should separate objective workplace facts from anxiety-driven interpretations before deciding how much the comments are contributing to your distress.
options.b: The comments sound discriminatory to me, so I do not want therapy to suggest that your distress is an overreaction.
options.c: Your panic is real even if the employees intended no harm. Let’s focus on the parts of the situation you can control clinically.
options.d: You’re questioning your own reaction while dealing with comments that have felt threatening and costly. What has this experience been like for you?

questions.question_text: Which inquiry BEST supports a cultural formulation of Fatima's workplace distress?

options.a: Ask how being targeted for hijab, religion, and accent affects belonging and whether Fatima wants the counselor to broach discrimination explicitly during treatment.
options.b: Explore migration, finances, professional identity, and workplace power first, then invite religion and gender if Fatima identifies them as relevant to the current problem.
options.c: Ask how hijab, religion, accent, migration, gender, professional identity, workplace power, belonging, and help-seeking intersect for Fatima while she decides which are central.
options.d: Explore prior experiences of bias and resilience, then compare them with the current workplace situation to identify culturally meaningful coping and support resources.

sections.stem:
Fatima is a 31-year-old engineer who has worked for the same firm for five years. She wears hijab and previously had strong performance reviews and no history of treatment for an anxiety disorder. About four months ago, after a supervisory change, she began receiving comments in meetings about her accent and religion. Her manager has asked whether her accent is “too strong for client presentations,” and a coworker has made jokes about whether her religious practices allow her to attend evening client events. Fatima says similar remarks have occurred several times and that the manager has not interrupted them.

During or just before meetings involving these coworkers, Fatima now experiences sudden episodes of racing heart, chest tightness, trembling, shortness of breath, dizziness, and fear that she will lose control. The episodes peak within several minutes. She has begun avoiding two recurring meetings and using email when possible. On Sunday evenings she often becomes tense and preoccupied with the coming workweek.

Fatima worries that making a formal workplace complaint could affect a pending immigration matter, but she has not received legal advice about that concern. She depends on her salary and employer-sponsored health insurance and has about six weeks of savings. She reports supportive friends. She denies suicidal or self-harm thoughts, mania, psychosis, and substance misuse. She asks, “Should I file a legal complaint?”

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Based on all information now available, which diagnosis is BEST supported?

options.a: Adjustment disorder with anxiety because symptoms followed ongoing workplace stressors and panic remains situationally cued rather than unexpected.
options.b: Panic disorder because recurrent panic, anticipatory worry, and meeting avoidance have persisted for months and now interfere with occupational functioning.
options.c: Social anxiety disorder because meetings involve scrutiny, possible negative evaluation, increasing avoidance, and meaningful impairment in her professional role.
options.d: Posttraumatic stress disorder because discriminatory comments produced avoidance, physiological arousal, anticipatory fear, and persistent impairment across her occupational functioning.

questions.question_text: Which treatment stance BEST integrates the cultural and contextual information in the case?

options.a: Integrate discrimination and workplace power into CBT, distinguish realistic threat from panic amplification, and target avoidance without requiring endurance of discriminatory conduct.
options.b: Use standard CBT and repeated meeting exposure while avoiding discussion of discrimination during practice so treatment currently remains focused on panic symptoms.
options.c: Encourage immediate formal reporting or legal action while symptoms are documented, then reassess whether anxiety persists after the workplace response unfolds.
options.d: Validate the discrimination-related stress and prioritize career advocacy, postponing anxiety treatment so realistic workplace threat is not pathologized.

questions.question_text: Which barrier should be given the GREATEST weight when the counselor and Fatima review whether she can act on her career goals now?

options.a: Lack of confidence is the main barrier because her technical skills and friendships are intact, making self-efficacy the central ongoing treatment target.
options.b: Panic symptoms are the main barrier, so career decision work should wait until Fatima can attend meetings without marked anticipatory anxiety.
options.c: Immigration and employment uncertainty, limited financial runway, and incomplete information most directly constrain informed career action; anxiety avoidance remains a parallel target.
options.d: The employer’s behavior is the main barrier, so treatment cannot progress meaningfully until the workplace comments stop or Fatima changes jobs.

questions.question_text: Which response BEST demonstrates respect and acceptance for diversity while preserving client autonomy?

options.a: Leaving may best protect your religious identity, while staying may require tolerating treatment that conflicts with your professional and personal values.
options.b: You do not need to prove your faith or career here; we can work from the identities, risks, and priorities that matter to you.
options.c: Assertiveness may be the key skill here; focusing heavily on religion or immigration during treatment could make the problem feel larger than it is.
options.d: Because financial stability is important, we should avoid options that could jeopardize employment until the legal and immigration situation becomes clearer.

questions.question_text: Which intervention plan BEST fits the current formulation?

options.a: Begin interoceptive exposure and cognitive restructuring now, but postpone workplace practice until the discrimination concern has been resolved through another resource.
options.b: Prioritize advocacy and career decision-making first because the anxiety should improve once Fatima has chosen whether to stay, transfer, or leave.
options.c: Use CBT for panic and anticipatory anxiety, graded return to selected legitimate work tasks, coping practice, and problem-solving around realistic risks and resources.
options.d: Use exposure in meetings where comments may recur, remaining until anxiety declines so Fatima learns that the workplace situation is emotionally tolerable over time.

sections.stem:
A primary-care evaluation, including physical examination and basic cardiac and thyroid screening, does not identify a medical explanation for the episodes. Fatima drinks one cup of coffee most mornings and reports no stimulant or illicit-substance use.

The panic episodes remain tied to workplace situations involving the manager or coworkers connected to the comments. She reports no unexpected attacks at home, while driving, in stores, or during sleep. She can give presentations at a professional association, meet new people, socialize, and shop without marked fear of scrutiny. She denies intrusive trauma memories, nightmares about the workplace events, or a persistent sense that unrelated settings are dangerous. Her worry is concentrated on work, finances, and the unresolved immigration question rather than on numerous areas of daily life.

The symptoms began within several weeks of the workplace comments intensifying and have continued for about four months, with increasing avoidance and occupational strain. Fatima says, “I don’t want therapy to teach me to tolerate being treated badly. I also don’t want fear making every career decision.” She has learned that an internal transfer may be available and that an employee-assistance/workplace resource can explain internal processes, but she has not yet consulted an employment or immigration attorney.

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: Given Fatima’s progress and new information, how should the treatment plan be revised?

options.a: Keep the current plan unchanged until Fatima makes a final employment decision, because changing goals now could interfere with the progress already established.
options.b: End structured anxiety work because panic has improved enough that the remaining concerns now belong primarily to career counseling.
options.c: Revise the plan toward residual anxiety, decision criteria, transfer or job-search actions, support use, continuity needs, and preservation of the gains already made.
options.d: Prioritize internal transfer as the next treatment objective because the new legal information and financial constraints make it the least disruptive option.

questions.question_text: Which conclusion BEST describes Fatima's current level of mental health functioning?

options.a: Fatima shows substantial improvement in anxiety-related work functioning and decision capacity, with residual workplace distress and uncertainty still creating meaningful strain.
options.b: Fatima's functioning is intact because she remains employed and is interviewing elsewhere; residual discrimination-related distress does not indicate clinical impairment.
options.c: Fatima remains substantially impaired because the employer's behavior is unresolved and her job choice remains uncertain despite reduced panic and avoidance.
options.d: Mental health functioning cannot be estimated until Fatima makes an employment decision and the legal or workplace processes have concluded.

questions.question_text: What is the counselor’s MOST appropriate response to Fatima’s requested letter?

options.a: Write the requested letter using Fatima’s allegations as clearly labeled client report, while stating that the workplace events are clinically consistent with causing her anxiety condition.
options.b: Decline any letter because once a workplace dispute involves legal issues, all treatment documentation becomes a forensic evaluation outside the counselor’s therapeutic role.
options.c: Provide a complete treatment summary or record release with authorization and allow the employer, attorney, or other recipient to draw any causation or legal conclusions.
options.d: Clarify the letter’s purpose and, with authorization, provide treatment, diagnosis, and functional observations; label workplace events as client-reported and decline unsupported causation or legal conclusions.

questions.question_text: Which counseling strategy BEST helps Fatima make the employment decision without directing the outcome?

options.a: Use a decision matrix for values, finances, qualified legal information, career growth, identity, health, risk, and reversibility; Fatima then chooses the next step.
options.b: Rank the available career options by which one is most likely to reduce Fatima’s anxiety symptoms and recommend the highest-scoring choice to her.
options.c: Recommend an internal transfer as a compromise because it preserves income while reducing contact with the manager connected to the comments for now.
options.d: Delay major career decisions until panic symptoms are in remission so anxiety does not distort Fatima’s judgment about employment options or long-term goals.

questions.question_text: Which termination discussion is MOST appropriate?

options.a: Continue counseling until Fatima's employment situation is fully settled because ending during an unresolved transition would create unnecessary recurrence risk.
options.b: End at the next session if Fatima reports no recent panic attacks, leaving career and legal resources available outside counseling if needed.
options.c: Review goals, response, feelings about ending, residual risks, supports, care continuity, and how Fatima can re-enter counseling if needs recur.
options.d: Transfer Fatima to a career-focused counselor before ending because an unresolved employment transition makes ordinary termination clinically premature.

sections.stem:
Eight weeks later, Fatima has re-entered selected legitimate work meetings using grounding, paced breathing, and agreed coping strategies. Panic episodes have decreased from about three per week to one in the past three weeks; anticipatory anxiety, avoidance, and sleep disruption have also improved. She continues to record workplace incidents for her own records.

Fatima has separately consulted a qualified immigration attorney about immigration questions and an employment attorney about workplace options and documentation. The consultations give her more accurate information but do not determine which career choice she should make. She remains employed, has requested consideration for an internal transfer, and has begun interviewing externally. She has not decided whether to remain, transfer, or leave.

Fatima asks the counselor to write a letter for human resources: “Please say that my employer caused my panic disorder and violated federal law.”

sections.title: SECTION 1 - INITIAL PRESENTATION
sections.heading: INITIAL PRESENTATION

questions.question_text: Which approach BEST represents an appropriate mental status examination?

options.a: Assess mood, sleep, speech, spending, and business judgment in detail, then defer orientation and perception because no psychotic symptoms are reported.
options.b: Assess appearance, behavior, psychomotor activity, speech, orientation, attention, thought process and content, perception, insight, judgment, and departure from baseline.
options.c: Compare Tasha's behavior with partner-reported baseline, emphasizing sleep, activity, and decision-making while leaving formal mental-status findings to the psychiatric evaluator.
options.d: Use a brief cognitive screen, observe attention and speech, and treat intact orientation as evidence that current judgment is likely preserved.

questions.question_text: Which substance and medication inquiry would provide the MOST useful diagnostic information?

options.a: Ask Tasha to stop cannabis for several days and compare symptoms before clarifying stimulant dose because cannabis can affect sleep and cognition.
options.b: Focus primarily on stimulant misuse because it is more directly relevant to activation, leaving stable nightly cannabis use for later assessment.
options.c: Review pharmacy records and prescriber notes first, then determine whether the stimulant exposure is sufficient to explain Tasha's behavioral change.
options.d: Clarify prescribed versus actual stimulant use, dose-change timing, cannabis and other substances, intended effects, consequences, tolerance, and relation to activation.

questions.question_text: Which assessment BEST determines whether Tasha's current level of mental health functioning is impaired?

options.a: Focus on financial losses and impulsive travel plans, because those consequences provide a more objective functional measure than mood or productivity changes.
options.b: Use the number of ventures launched and hours worked as primary indicators, because preserved productivity would argue against substantial functional impairment.
options.c: Compare Tasha's self-report with her partner's observations and consider functioning intact when both agree she is completing essential daily responsibilities.
options.d: Evaluate spending, contracts, driving, sleep, follow-through, relationships, occupational consequences, and ability to reconsider decisions compared with Tasha's usual functioning.

questions.question_text: Which immediate disposition is MOST proportionate to the information currently available?

options.a: Arrange same-day psychiatric evaluation with safe transportation, recommend no driving, travel, or major commitments pending assessment, and coordinate with prescriber and support.
options.b: Recommend voluntary psychiatric hospitalization now because markedly reduced sleep, overspending, and risky travel show that outpatient treatment cannot safely contain the episode.
options.c: Arrange prescriber contact within forty-eight hours, ask Tasha's partner to monitor sleep and spending, and continue frequent outpatient counseling until evaluation.
options.d: Initiate involuntary emergency evaluation because impaired judgment, overspending, and planned cross-country travel establish inability to participate safely in voluntary care.

sections.stem:
Tasha is a 29-year-old entrepreneur who has received treatment for ADHD from an outside prescriber for approximately six years. She describes her usual baseline as energetic and ambitious but says she normally sleeps seven hours, maintains one primary business at a time, consults others before major purchases, and is able to slow down when a plan does not make financial sense.

During the past 10 days, Tasha has slept approximately two and a half to three hours per night and says she is “not tired at all.” She has launched plans for three new businesses, purchased approximately $12,000 in equipment, and contacted several potential investors. She speaks rapidly and frequently shifts topics while describing an idea she says will “change the entire industry.”

Her prescribed stimulant is taken each morning for ADHD. Tasha acknowledges that during the past several days she has sometimes taken additional medication beyond the prescribed dose because she believes it helps her “keep up with all the ideas.” She also reports nightly cannabis use.

Tasha denies suicidal or homicidal thoughts and reports no hallucinations. She plans to drive across several states the following morning to meet an investor, although the investor has not confirmed the meeting. Her partner says the current behavior is “way beyond her normal ambitious.”

sections.title: SECTION 2 - ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
sections.heading: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

questions.question_text: Which provisional formulation is BEST supported by the longitudinal evidence?

options.a: Bipolar I disorder, current manic episode, with stimulant misuse as a possible exacerbating factor rather than the sole explanation for the episode.
options.b: Substance/medication-induced bipolar and related disorder, because stimulant overuse occurred during the episode and stimulants can produce manic symptoms in susceptible individuals.
options.c: Bipolar II disorder, current hypomanic episode, because Tasha remains oriented, has no psychosis, and continues managing basic responsibilities despite substantial activation.
options.d: ADHD with stimulant misuse and sleep deprivation, because distractibility, rapid activity, impulsive projects, and reduced sleep can intensify when stimulant dosing increases.

questions.question_text: Which collaboration plan is MOST appropriate at this point?

options.a: Ask Tasha's partner to contact the prescriber because collateral information is more reliable during mania, while the counselor focuses on maintaining Tasha's alliance.
options.b: Tell the prescriber the stimulant likely caused the episode and recommend stopping it immediately, while asking the partner to monitor Tasha until symptoms resolve.
options.c: With Tasha's permission, share the symptom timeline, MSE findings, actual stimulant and cannabis use, functional risks, and collateral information with the evaluator and prescriber.
options.d: Wait for the psychiatric evaluator to request records before communicating, because proactive coordination could influence the evaluator's independent diagnostic judgment and treatment planning.

questions.question_text: Tasha says, “I'm scared everyone will start calling my ambition an illness.” Which response BEST demonstrates empathic attunement?

options.a: Your ambition is not the problem. The issue is the manic episode, and we can learn to separate the two once your mood stabilizes.
options.b: It sounds frightening that concern about your mood feels like people are dismissing the ambition you value. Can we compare this with your usual drive?
options.c: Many entrepreneurs sleep less and take risks when building something new, so we should be careful not to pathologize traits that may help you succeed.
options.d: The spending and sleep changes show this is more than ordinary ambition. Understanding that difference will help you protect the business goals that matter.

questions.question_text: Which inquiry BEST addresses cultural and contextual considerations in Tasha's presentation?

options.a: Explore how gender, entrepreneurship culture, family expectations, stigma, and prior mental-health experiences shape Tasha's understanding of productivity and treatment without assuming causation.
options.b: Explore whether gender bias in entrepreneurship explains why others view Tasha as unstable, then use advocacy to prevent confident behavior from being pathologized.
options.c: Keep cultural issues separate from diagnosis until the acute episode resolves, because identity-based interpretations could bias assessment of objective manic symptoms.
options.d: Ask Tasha's family what level of work intensity and confidence is typical in their culture, then use that information to establish her premorbid baseline.

questions.question_text: Which temporary strategy BEST protects Tasha's decision-making while preserving as much autonomy as possible?

options.a: Ask Tasha to give her partner temporary control of business accounts, credit cards, travel bookings, and contracts until the psychiatric team determines the episode has resolved.
options.b: Have Tasha continue business activity while using a daily mood tracker and postponing major decisions only after nights when she sleeps less than four hours.
options.c: Freeze all new ventures and travel until psychiatric clearance, while allowing routine business tasks that do not involve spending, contracts, or public commitments.
options.d: Collaboratively choose temporary safeguards such as delaying major commitments, trusted review of high-impact decisions, safer transportation, sleep protection, and clear escalation steps.

sections.stem:
Further assessment clarifies that Tasha's longstanding ADHD symptoms primarily involve distractibility, disorganization, difficulty completing routine tasks, and procrastination. At baseline, she does not experience sustained periods of markedly elevated mood, dramatically increased goal-directed activity, or a reduced need for sleep.

The current change began 10 days ago. Tasha first began sleeping only three hours, speaking rapidly, generating multiple business plans, and feeling unusually powerful and productive. Five days into that change, she began taking approximately twice her prescribed stimulant dose without consulting the prescriber.

Her cannabis pattern—one nightly edible—has been essentially unchanged for about six months. She denies other drugs, nonprescribed stimulants, energy products, or heavy caffeine use.

Tasha's partner describes another distinct episode three years ago, during a period when Tasha had been off stimulant medication for approximately two months and was not using cannabis. For nine days she slept only two to three hours without fatigue, spoke much more rapidly than usual, became unusually expansive and irritable, spent approximately $8,000 on an abrupt business venture, and quit a stable job with little planning. Her functioning deteriorated enough that family members intervened financially. No psychiatric evaluation occurred at the time.

Tasha later experienced a six-week period of marked depression, loss of interest, low energy, excessive sleep, and difficulty functioning. Her mother has bipolar I disorder.

During the current examination Tasha is oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Her speech is pressured, her thoughts move rapidly between loosely connected business ideas, and she is easily distracted. She reports no hallucinations or fixed delusions. Insight into the degree of change is limited, and judgment regarding spending, driving, and business commitments appears impaired.

Tasha agrees to same-day psychiatric evaluation and permits communication with her prescriber and evaluator. She authorizes her partner to assist with transportation and with temporary safeguards they agree upon.

She later says, “Women entrepreneurs get called unstable for being confident all the time. My family taught me to work hard and be independent. I don't want everyone treating every ambitious idea like a symptom.”

sections.title: SECTION 3 - COURSE OF CARE
sections.heading: COURSE OF CARE

questions.question_text: Which pre/post measurement approach would provide the STRONGEST evidence of change after Tasha's acute episode?

options.a: Compare medication adherence and sleep with the acute episode baseline, adding broader mood and functioning measures only if either begins to worsen again.
options.b: Use partner ratings and financial records before and after stabilization because those provide the most objective evidence of change in judgment and functioning.
options.c: Repeat the same mood or activation and functioning measures at planned intervals, comparing with baseline plus sleep, spending, commitments, substance use, depression, and judgment.
options.d: Shift to ADHD measures after mood stabilization and use psychiatric progress notes for bipolar outcomes so counseling measurement remains focused on Tasha's ongoing diagnosis.

questions.question_text: Which treatment-plan revision BEST fits Tasha's current course?

options.a: Revise the plan around recurrence prevention, shame and financial repair, ADHD reassessment with prescribers, and distinguishing healthy ambition from episode-related change.
options.b: Return to ADHD-focused counseling because acute mood activation has resolved, while using psychiatric follow-up only if another clear manic episode develops.
options.c: Shift counseling toward rebuilding finances and business confidence, leaving bipolar recurrence management and ADHD decisions primarily to the psychiatric treatment team.
options.d: Advise Tasha to avoid launching new businesses for six months while she learns which levels of energy and confidence are safe outside acute treatment.

questions.question_text: Which documentation BEST supports continuity and review of Tasha's acute episode?

Five weeks later, Tasha reports sleeping seven to eight hours most nights. Her speech and thought process are again near her usual baseline. She has made no further large purchases or impulsive travel plans, has withdrawn several unrealistic business commitments, and has resumed routine work on her existing company.

She continues coordinated psychiatric care. Her ADHD symptoms remain relevant and will be reassessed by her prescribing clinicians after mood stabilization. Tasha has also worked with the treatment team on her cannabis use.

Tasha reports embarrassment and grief about the $12,000 loss and says, “Now I second-guess every good idea. I don't want to become afraid of being successful.”
